# Chapter 4. IV. Of the New Rebirth.

...lamenting, hungering, and thirsting for the sweet **fountain of Christ**: such a person finds refreshment through hungering and desiring—which is the true faith—in the sweet **fountain of Christ**, receiving from his new body of heavenly essence, like a hungry branch on the vine of **Christ**.

13. And this is the reason why the fiery soul <note>In Böhme’s theology, the "fiery soul" represents the first principle of human nature—the raw, consuming will that must be tempered by light.</note> cannot reach perfection during this life: because it remains tied to the outer bond of vanity <note>In this context, "vanity" refers to the temporary, illusory, and corruptible nature of the material world.</note>, through which the devil constantly shoots his poisonous rays at it and sifts it. This causes the soul to sometimes "bite" at the bait and poison itself, leading to great misery and anxiety. Because of this, the noble **Sophia** <note>Sophia, or Divine Wisdom, is depicted here as the soul's celestial bride who represents the lost divine image.</note> hides herself in the **fountain of Christ** within heavenly humanity and will not approach the vanity.

14. For she knows how it went for her in **Adam**, when she lost her pearl <note>The "pearl" is a common mystical metaphor for the hidden spark of divinity or the kingdom of God within the heart.</note>; this pearl is restored to the inner humanity through grace (which is why she is called **Sophia**, as the bride of **Christ**).

15. Here, she faithfully calls to the fiery soul as if to her bridegroom, and exhorts him to repentance and refreshment, or to a departure from the abomination of vanity. Then the struggle begins within the whole person; the outer, fleshly man lusts against the inner, spiritual man, and the spiritual against the fleshly; and so the person stands in conflict, full of tribulation, sorrow, anxiety, and distress.

16. The inner voice says to the fiery soul: "O my beloved <note>original: "Buhle"; while this can mean "paramour" in modern German, in 17th-century mystical writing it refers to a deeply loved spiritual partner or sweetheart.</note>, turn back now and depart from vanity, or you will lose my love and the noble pearl." But the outer reason—the animal (<gloss>or earthly</gloss>) soul—says: "You are a fool to want to be the world's fool and laughingstock! You need the outer world for your life. Beauty, power, and glory are what is best for you, and in them you can have joy. Why would you lead yourself into anxiety, distress, and mockery? Seek after pleasure, which does good to the flesh and the mind."

17. A true human being is often defiled with such filth; the outer man defiles himself just like a sow in the mud and darkens his noble image. For the more "vain" the outer man becomes, the darker the inner man grows, until he eventually fades away entirely. When that happens, it is all over for the beautiful **little Paradise-tree** <note>A metaphor for the growing spiritual life within the believer.</note>, and it will be difficult to regain.

### Chapter 5.

#### Summaries.

The **mouth-Christian** <note>A "mouth-Christian" is someone who professes faith with words but lacks inner transformation.</note> is only **Babel** <note>In this context, "Babel" represents the confusion of worldly, institutional religion that lacks true spiritual power.</note> and a chatterer. 6. For Christ belongs only to the repentant, but not to the **beast** <note>The "beast" refers to the animalistic, fallen nature of man.</note>. 11. He wishes only to have newborn children, 12. who are not of this world. 13. Then our way of life is in heaven, and Christ is our heaven within us. 14.

At this point, a Christian should reflect on why he calls himself a Christian, and consider well whether he truly is one. For simply learning to know and understand that I am a sinner, and that Christ killed my sin on the **cross** and shed his blood for me, does not by any means make a Christian out of me; the **inheritance** belongs only to the children. A maid in the house well knows what the mistress likes, but that does not make her an heir to the mistress's goods. The devil also knows that there is a God, but that does not make him an angel again; however, if the maid in the house marries the mistress’s son, she may indeed come into the inheritance of the mistress’s goods.

2. This is also to be understood regarding our Christianity. The "children of history" <note>original: "Historien Kinder"; those who know the literal facts of scripture but lack the inner spiritual experience</note> are not heirs to the goods of Christ; rather, the legitimate children are those who are born anew from Christ's Spirit. For God said to Abraham: *Cast out the son of the bondwoman, for he shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.* **Galatians 4:30.** For he was a mocker, and only a "son of history" regarding the faith and spirit of Abraham. 4. Therefore, everyone who wishes to call himself a Christian must cast out the "son of the bondwoman"—that is, the earthly, evil will—and must constantly kill and break it. Instead, like our father Abraham, we must lead the son of our righteous will to Mount Moriah and be willing to sacrifice him to God in obedience. We must always desire to die to sin in Christ’s death, allowing the "beast of vanity" no rest in Christ’s kingdom. We must not let it become wanton, proud, greedy, envious, or malicious. All these qualities belong to Ishmael, the son of the bondwoman, whom Adam—in his vanity—bore in the flesh from the earthly nature, through the "wanton harlot" of the false bondwoman and the **devil’s imagination** <note>original: "Teufels Imagination"; here, the power of the mind to be shaped by or "pictured" into sinful, worldly desires.</note>.

# IV. Of the New Rebirth. Chapter 5.

...mouth-hypocrisy and sham holiness; and yet is only a bloodthirsty murderer of Abel <note>original: "Habels"; Böhme uses the biblical Cain and Abel as archetypes for the false and true believer.</note> his brother, who is a true heir.

6. Therefore we say, as we have recognized it, that a person who wishes to call himself a Christian should examine what kind of qualities drive and rule him; whether the Spirit of Christ drives him toward truth, righteousness, and love for his neighbor, so that he would gladly do good if he only knew how. And if he finds that he has a hunger for such virtue, he may certainly think that he is being "drawn" <note>A reference to John 6:44, where the Father "draws" the soul to Christ.</note>; thus he should put it into practice, not only willing it but not doing it. So it is also with the children of God: they have various gifts and knowledge, but all from the same Spirit. They rejoice alongside one another in the great wonders of God and thank the Most High in His wisdom. Why should they wrangle for long about Him in whom they live and are, and of whose essence they themselves consist?

## IV. Of the New Rebirth. Chapter 7.

8. It is the greatest folly in Babel <note>Babel: In this context, a symbolic term for the confusion, pride, and division found in institutionalized religions that prioritize dogma over spiritual life.</note> that the devil has made the world quarrelsome concerning religion, so that they fight over self-made opinions and the literal word; whereas the Kingdom of God consists in no opinion, but in power and love. Christ also said, and left it to His disciples at the last, that they should love one another; by this, everyone would recognize that they were His disciples, just as He had loved them. If people sought love and righteousness as much as they sought opinions, there would be no strife at all on earth; we would live as children in our Father and would need no law nor order.

9. For God is served by no law, but by obedience alone. Laws exist for the sake of the wicked, who do not desire love and righteousness; they are driven and compelled by laws. We all have one single Order, which is that we remain still before the Lord of all beings, surrender our will to Him, and let His Spirit work, play, and do in us what He wills; and what He works and reveals in us, we offer back to Him as His fruit.

10. If we did not quarrel about the various fruits, gifts, and knowledge, but recognized each other as children of the Spirit of God, what would there be to judge us? For the Kingdom of God does not depend on our knowing and imagining, but in the power.

11. If we did not know half as much and were much more childlike <note>original: "kindischer"; used here to mean the humble, simple, and trusting nature of a child rather than being "immature."</note>, yet had only a brotherly will toward one another and lived as children of one mother—like the branches on a tree that all draw sap from one root—we would be much holier.

12. Knowledge is only for this end (that we might learn it) because we have lost the Divine Power in Adam <note>The "Adam" reference pertains to the biblical Fall of Man, which the author views as the moment humanity lost its direct, powerful connection to the divine nature.</note>, and are now so inclined toward evil that we must learn to recognize it—how we have evil qualities within us and that evil deeds do not please God—so that through knowledge we might learn to do right. # Chapter 8. IV. Of the New Rebirth.

13. ...forth as children, just as the earth brings forth many kinds of flowers. Therefore, those people who argue about knowledge <note>original: "Wissenschaft"; in this context, it refers to systematic theology or intellectual learning rather than modern science</note> and God’s will, and who despise one another for it, are more foolish than the birds in the forest and the wild animals, which have no proper understanding. 15. In summary, they are the devil's growth in the wrath of God, who must nonetheless serve the Lord through their own torment. For by their plague and persecution, they drive the "sap" through the essence of the children of God, so that these children move within the Spirit of God with prayer and diligent pleading, in which the Spirit of God moves within them. For the spiritual desire is exercised by this, as are the children of God, so that they may turn green and bear fruit; for in tribulation, God’s children are made manifest, according to the Scripture: *When you chastise them, they call out to you in their anxiety.*

...has His power within himself? Christ speaks plainly: The sheep do not hear his (the false shepherd’s) voice; they do not follow him. John 10:5.

6. The written word is only a tool that the Spirit guides. The word that seeks to teach must be alive within the literal word: God's Spirit must be within the literal sound <note>original: "Halle"; literally the resonance or sound of the voice</note>, otherwise no one is a teacher of God, but only a teacher of letters, a knower of histories, and not of God's Spirit in Christ. Everything with which one wants to serve God must happen in faith, as in the Spirit, who makes the work complete and pleasing before God. Whatever a person begins and does in faith, they do in the Spirit of God, who works together in the deed; that is pleasing to God; for He has made it Himself, and His power is within it; it is holy.

7. But whatever is done in selfhood <term>Selbheit: Böhme’s term for the egoistic, self-centered nature of fallen man that acts independently of God</term> without faith is only a figure or an aid <note>or a mere shadow</note> of a true Christian work.

8. If you serve your brother and do so only out of hypocrisy <term>Gleißnerey: an archaic term for false piety or "glittering" outward holiness that masks an empty interior</term>, and you give to him reluctantly, then you do not serve God. For your faith does not proceed from love into hope within your gift. Indeed, you serve your brother, and he for his part thanks God and also blesses you for his part; but you do not bless him, for you give him a grumbling spirit in your gift, which does not enter into God’s Spirit, into the hope of faith: therefore your gift is only half-given, and you have only half a reward for it.

9. The same is to be understood regarding receiving. If one gives in faith in Divine hope, he blesses his gifts in his faith; but he who receives them ungratefully and grumbles in his spirit, curses them in the enjoyment <term>Nießung: the act of consuming, using, or partaking in a benefit</term>: thus to each remains his own; what he sows, he also reaps.

10. So it is also in the office of teaching <term>Lehr-Amt: the formal vocation of preaching or religious instruction</term>: what one sows, he also reaps. If one sows good seed from the Spirit of Christ, it takes root <note>original: "bekleibt"; an archaic term meaning to stick, adhere, or thrive</note> in the good heart and bears good fruit; but in the godless, who are not capable of receiving it, the wrath of God is provoked. If one sows strife, contempt, and misinterpretation, all godless people take it in; it also takes root and bears such fruit that people mock, deride, slander, and misinterpret one another.

Thus he stands in GOD’S field and bears fruit on GOD’S table, which he shall enjoy eternally. Amen.

1. The Disciple said to the Master: How may I come to the supersensual life, that I may see God and hear Him speak? The Master said: When you can swing yourself for one moment into that place where no creature dwells, then you hear what God speaks.

2. The Disciple said: Is that near or far? The Master said: It is in you; and if you can be silent from all your willing and thinking for one hour, then you will hear the inexpressible words of God.

3. The Disciple said: How can I hear, if I stand still from senses and will? The Master said: When you stand still from the thinking and willing of your selfhood <term>Selbheit: the state of being focused on one's own ego or private interest</term>, then the eternal hearing, seeing, and speaking will be made manifest in you, and God hears and sees through you; your own hearing, willing, and seeing prevents you, so that you do not see nor hear God.

4. The Disciple said: With what shall I hear and see God, since He is above nature and creature? The Master said: When you are silent, then you are that which God was before nature and creature, out of which He created your nature and creature: then you hear and see it with that which God saw and heard in you, before your own willing, seeing, and hearing began.

5. The Disciple said: What holds me back then, that I may not reach that point? The Master said: Your own willing, hearing, and seeing; and the fact that you strive against that from which you came. With your own will, you break yourself off from God's will, and with your own seeing, you see only into your own willing; and your willing stops your hearing with the self-centeredness <note>original: *Eigensinnlichkeit*</note> of earthly, natural things.

6. The Disciple said: Since I exist within nature, how may I come through nature into the supersensual foundation without the breaking of nature? The Master said: Three things are required for this. The first is that you surrender your will to God, and sink yourself to the very bottom into His mercy. The second is that you hate your own will, and do not do that which your will drives you toward. But if you have left the pictorial nature, then you stand in the state of beyond-imaging <term>Ueberbildlichkeit: a state of being "above images," where the soul perceives the essence of things directly rather than through mental pictures or physical forms</term>, and you rule in the foundation over all creatures from which they were created. Then nothing on earth may harm you, for you are equal with all things, and nothing is unequal to you.

# V. On the Supersensual Life.

...the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, when He spoke: "Unless you turn and become as children, you shall not see God’s kingdom." Matthew 18:3. If it is now your wish to become equal to all things, then you must forsake all things; you must turn your desire away from them and not long for them, nor accept anything as a possession that is "Something." For as soon as you grasp that "Something" in your desire, and let it into yourself to hold as your own, then that "Something" becomes one with you. It works with you within your own will, and you are then obligated to protect it and care for it as if it were your own essence. But if you take nothing into your desire, then you are free from all things and rule over all things at once. For you hold nothing in your appropriation <note>original: *Annehmlichkeit*; in this context, the act of taking things into oneself as personal property</note>, and you are a "Nothing" to all things, and all things are likewise a "Nothing" to you. You are like a child who does not understand what a "thing" is; and even if you do understand it, you understand it without it touching your sensitivity, in the same way that God rules and sees all things, and yet no thing can grasp Him. 

But as for what you said—that I should teach you how you might reach this state—look to the words of Christ, who spoke: "Without me you can do nothing." John 15:5. You cannot come to such peace through your own power, where no creature can touch you, unless you surrender yourself entirely into the life of our Lord Jesus Christ. You must give over your willing and your desire entirely to Him, and will nothing without Him. Then you will stand with your body in the world among its various qualities, and with your reason <note>original: *Vernunft*</note> under the cross of our Lord Christ; but with your will, you walk in heaven. You stand at the "End"—the source from which all creatures came and to which they return. Thus, you may look upon everything outwardly with your reason, and look upon everything inwardly with your soul <note>original: *Gemüthe*; the inner disposition or spiritual mind</note>, and—with Christ, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth—rule in and over all things. Matthew 28:18.

But as for what you said—why the ungodly do not feel Hell at this time—I say: They do feel it in their false conscience, but they do not understand it, for they still have the earthly vanity which they love, and in which they find joy and pleasure. Also, the outer life still possesses the light of outer nature, in which the soul takes its delight, so that the torment cannot yet be revealed. But when the body dies, the soul can no longer enjoy such temporal pleasures, and the light of the outer world is extinguished for it. Then it stands in eternal thirst and hunger for the same vanity in which it delighted here, but it can reach nothing except that same false, self-enclosed will. Of that will, it had too much in this life and yet could not be satisfied; now, it has too little. Therefore, it is in eternal hunger and thirst for vanity, malice, and frivolousness. It would always gladly do more evil, but has nothing in which or with which it can perform it, so this "performance" happens only within itself. Such hellish hunger and thirst cannot become fully manifest within it until the body dies—the body with which it lusted after pleasure and which provided what it craved.

All rising up of pride, where one strives only over <term>opinions|Meynungen; here referring to sectarian dogmas or intellectual theories about God</term>, is an image of self-interest. Whoever does not have faith and humility, and does not stand in Christ’s Spirit, is armed only with the wrath of God; he serves the victory of that "image-based" selfhood, which is the kingdom of darkness and the wrath of God. For all selfhood will be given to the darkness on the Day of Judgment: as will their useless bickering, through which they seek no love, but only a "pictorial" selfhood—to make themselves seen in their opinions, and thereby cause princes to go to war over such imaginary opinions, and with their "images" storm and devastate land and people. These all belong in the Judgment to be separated, the false from the right; there all images and opinions shall cease, and all children of God shall walk in the love of Christ, and He in us. Everything in this time of strife that does not zealously act in the Spirit of Christ, and does not desire to promote love alone, but seeks self-interest in the struggle—that is from the Devil, and belongs to the darkness, and will be separated from Christ: for in heaven everything serves God its Creator in humility.

57. **The disciple spoke:** Why then does God allow such strife to happen in this time? The Master spoke:

<vocab>Christ, Devil, selfhood, pride, opinions, faith, humility, kingdom of Christ, darkness, Judgment Day, Creator</vocab>

<header>V. On the Supersensual Life.</header>

...spoke: Life exists in conflict, so that it may become manifest, perceptible, and findable, and so that Wisdom may be discerned and recognized; and this serves for the eternal joy of overcoming. For in the saints in Christ, a great praise will arise from this: that Christ has overcome the darkness and all <term>selfhood|Eigenheit; the self-centered nature of the ego that seeks its own power over God’s will</term> of nature within them, and they are delivered from the conflict. In this they will eternally rejoice, when they perceive how the ungodly are repaid. Thus God lets all things stand in free will, so that the eternal dominion according to love and wrath, light and darkness, may be revealed and known, and each life may cause and awaken its own judgment within itself. For what is now a conflict and pain for the saints in their misery shall be transformed for them into great joy; and what is a pleasure and joy for the ungodly in this world shall be turned for them into eternal pain and shame. And therefore, the joy of the saints must arise out of death, just as the light from a candle arises through the dying and consuming in the fire, so that life may thus become free from the <note>original: "Peinlichkeit" - Böhme uses this to describe the "agonizing" or "striving" quality of material nature that feels itself as a painful tension until it finds the light</note> anguish of nature, and possess another world. Just as light has a completely different quality than fire—for light gives of itself, while fire takes and devours—so also the holy life of gentleness blossoms forth through death, where the self-will dies, and God's will of love alone governs and acts in all things.

For in this way, the Eternal has taken on perceptibility and distinctness, and through death has led itself out again with that perceptibility into a great kingdom of joy, so that there may be an eternal play in the infinite Unity, and an eternal cause for the kingdom of joy. Thus, the anguish must be the ground and cause of such movement.

And in this lies the <term>mystery|Mysterium</term> of the hidden wisdom of God.

He who asks, receives; he who seeks, finds; and to him who knocks, it shall be opened. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with us all. Amen.

# VI. On Divine Contemplation. Chapter 1.

Reason speaks: I hear much said of God—that there is a God who has created all things, and who also sustains and carries all things; but I have not yet seen any man, nor heard of one, who has seen God, or who could say where God dwells or exists, or what He is like. For when Reason looks upon the nature of this world and considers how it goes for the godly just as it does for the wicked, and how all things are mortal and fragile—and how the godly man sees no savior to deliver him from the anguish and opposition <note>original: "Widerwärtigkeit"</note> of evil, and thus must go to the pit <note>The "pit" (Grube) traditionally refers to the grave or the state of death.</note> with anxieties in misery—then it thinks all things happen by chance. It thinks there is no God who takes an interest in the sufferer, because He leaves the one who hopes in Him stuck in misery to go into the pit, and because one has never heard of anyone who has returned from corruption <note>original: "Verwesung" — the state of bodily decay after death.</note> and said that he had been with God.

2. Answer: Reason is a natural life, whose foundation <term>Grund|The underlying basis or essential nature of a thing</term> stands in a temporal beginning and end, and it cannot enter into the supernatural foundation in which God is understood. For even though Reason looks upon itself in this world and finds no other foundation in its contemplation, it nevertheless feels within itself a longing for a higher foundation in which it might find rest.

3. For Reason understands that it has come from a supernatural foundation, and that there must be a God who has brought it into life and willing. It is terrified within itself by its own will toward wickedness; it is ashamed within itself of its own willing, and judges itself as "unright" in the willing of evil. Even if it does what is unright, it still accuses itself and fears a judgment <term>Gericht|The divine court or trial of the soul</term> that it does not see. This indicates that the hidden God, who has brought Himself into Nature, dwells within Reason and punishes it for the evil way—and that this same hidden God must not be of the nature of sensory perception <note>original: "Empfindlichkeit"</note>, because Reason neither sees nor grasps Him.

### Chapter 1. VI. On Divine Contemplation.

4. In contrast, the abandoned reason—which feels itself (in its own estimation) wrongly tormented in misery—feels a desire within itself to abandon itself even more. <meta>This page continues the exploration of the divine nature and its manifestation through contrast. ### VI. On Divine Contemplation. Chapter 1.

**God is unperceived by the natural life.** Even if there were no adversity in life, there would also be no sensation, nor any willing or acting; neither would there be understanding or knowledge. For a thing that has only *one* will has no differentiation <term>Schiedlichkeit: A central term in Böhme’s thought, referring to the state of being distinct, divided, or manifold, which allows for contrast and perception.</term>. If it does not feel an opposing will to stir it into motion, it remains still. For a single thing knows nothing more than one; and even if it is good in itself, it knows neither evil nor good, for it has nothing within itself to make it sensible <note>In this context, "sensible" means the capacity to feel or perceive through contrast.</note>.

10. In this way, we can also philosophize about the will of GOD and say: If the hidden God—who is only one single Essence and Will—had not moved His will out of Himself, and if He had not brought Himself out of eternal Knowledge in the *temperamento* <note>original: "Temperamento" — referring to a state of perfect balance or harmony where all qualities are unified and none is dominant.</note> into the differentiation of the will, and if He had not brought that same differentiation into a tangibility <note>original: "Infaßlichkeit" — the quality of being graspable or contained within a form.</note> for a natural and creaturely life—and if that same differentiation in life did not stand in conflict—how then would the hidden will of God, which in itself is only One, be revealed to Him? How can there be a knowledge of oneself in a single, unified will?

11. But because there is a differentiation in the One Will, so that the differentiation leads into centers and self-wills <note>original: "Eigenwillen" — the individual will that seeks its own way rather than the universal divine will.</note>—so that in that which is separated there is a will of its own, and thus in one single Will unfathomable and innumerable wills arise, like branches from a tree—so we see and understand that in such differentiation, every separated will leads itself into its own form. The conflict of the wills is over the form, for one form in its partiality is not like the other, and yet they all stand in one Ground.

12. For a single will cannot break itself into pieces; just as the mind <term>Gemüthe: The deep inner disposition of a person, encompassing the heart, soul, and intellect.</term> does not break into pieces when it divides into a bad and a good willing. Instead, the output of the senses <note>original: "Sensuum" — Latin for "of the senses."</note> only separates into a bad and a good willing, while the mind remains whole within itself and suffers <note>In the archaic sense of "permits" or "endures."</note> both a bad and a good willing to arise and dwell within it.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of how the Divine Will reveals itself through the interplay of opposites. It builds on the previous page's discussion of why the "hidden God" must move into differentiation to be perceived, now specifically addressing the role of evil or adversity as the necessary friction that allows the Good to become active and self-aware.</meta>

### Chapter 1. VI. On Divine Contemplation.

13. Thus **Reason** speaks: To what end or use is it that evil must exist alongside the good? **Answer**: Evil, or the opposing will, causes the good—namely the will—to press back toward its origin <term>Urstand: A foundational state or original source of being.</term>, toward **GOD**, and causes the good (as the good will) to become desirous. For a thing that is only good in itself and has no torment <note>The original word is "Qual." In Böhme's thought, this implies both "torment" and "quality/source-force," suggesting that without friction or pain, there is no drive or life.</note> desires nothing; for it knows of nothing better within or before itself for which it could long.

14. Thus we can also philosophize regarding the single good will of **GOD** and say that He can desire nothing within Himself, for He has nothing within or before Him that could give Him anything. He therefore leads Himself out of Himself into a differentiation <term>Schiedlichkeit: The state of being distinct, divided, or manifold; the process by which unity becomes plurality.</term>, into **centers**, so that an opposition might arise in the outflow—that is, in that which has flowed forth—so that the good might become perceptible, active, and willing within the evil; namely, by wanting to separate itself from the evil and wanting to enter back into the single will of **GOD**.

15. But because the outflow of the single eternal will of **GOD** continually proceeds out of itself toward its revelation, the good (as the divine power) also flows out from the Eternal One with such an outflow and enters into the differentiation and the **centers** of multiplicity.

16. Thus, the perpetual outflow of the will, with its motion, causes the good within it to yearn for stillness again and to become desirous of pressing back into the Eternal One. In such a pressing-back into itself, the One becomes mobile and desirous; and within such an operation lie perception, knowledge, and willing.

17. **GOD**, insofar as He is called **GOD**, can will nothing but Himself; for He has nothing before or after Him that He can will. But if He wills something, that thing has flowed out from Him and is a counterpart <note>original: "Gegenwurf" — literally a "throwing-against," meaning an object, reflection, or projection of the self.</note> of Himself, wherein the Eternal Will wills within its "Something." If this "Something" were only one single thing, the will would have no accomplishment within it; and therefore the bottomless <note>original: "ungründliche" — referring to the *Ungrund*, Böhme’s concept of the absolute divine abyss or groundless will that precedes all existence.</note> will has divided itself into beginnings and enclosed itself in essences so that it might act within "Something," just as one sees an analogy in the human mind.

18. If the mind did not flow out from itself, then

### VI. On Divine Contemplation. Chapter 1.

[...eternal will, it] would have no senses; but if it had no senses, it would have no knowledge of itself, nor of any other thing, and could have no completion or effect. But the sensory outflow from the mind <term>Gemüth: The soul-mind; the deep seat of will, emotion, and thought.</term> (which is a reflection <term>Gegenwurf: Literally a "counter-throw"; an objective projection or mirror-image in which the subject can perceive itself.</term> of the mind, wherein the mind perceives itself) makes the mind willing or desiring, so that the mind leads the senses into something, as into a center of selfhood <term>Ichheit: "I-hood" or egoity; the state of being an individual self.</term>, wherein the mind works through the senses and, in working with the senses, reveals and contemplates itself.

It must accept this grace and, in the power of such acceptance and divine union, sink itself with its surrendered life-will into the **supersensory** <note>original: "übersinnliche"</note> and **unfathomable** <note>original: "übergründliche"</note> **Eternal One**, as if into the first ground of life's beginning. By giving itself back into the Ground from which life first sprouted, it is then back in its eternal place, in the **harmony of qualities** <note>original: "Temperamento"</note>, and in true rest.

17. Through this speaking-into, God's will takes hold of his own will and speaks into the figurative, natural, essential, outer **reason-life**. It shatters and illuminates the earthly formation of the **reason-will**, so that immediately the **supersensory Divine life and will** blooms and **centers itself** <note>original: "eincentriret"</note> within the reason-will.

18. For just as the life’s own will—in its selfhood and in a will turned away from God—cannot stand still for a single moment from its own activity in nature (unless it sinks itself outside of all nature), so too the **Divine Speaking** in a life surrendered to its ground cannot stand still from its working.

### Chapter 2. VI. On Divine Contemplation. 183 ###

New Rebirth—or the Divine Will made active and manifest in such a life—is required; for as long as a person stands in the earthly will alone, they are no child of heaven. For the **Divine Science** <note>original: "Scienz"; in Böhme’s vocabulary, this refers to a deep, inherent knowledge or the "craft" of divine wisdom within the soul.</note> is transformed into earthly, animalistic properties through the self-shaping of the false will. Such a person is, according to the body, an evil beast, and according to the soul, a turned-away false will that does not want what God wants—much like the devils, who also exist within their own shaping of sensory knowledge.

24. Therefore Christ said: **Matthew 12, 30. "He who does not gather with me"** <note>original: "Wer nicht mit mir sammelt"</note>—that is, whoever does not work, will, and act with the embodied grace of God (which God has revealed and offered through Christ), but instead works through their own natural will, "scatters." Such a person scatters not only the Divine order of the senses, but also sows their works into a false ground.

25. Consider an analogy from the sun. When a plant has no sap, the sun’s ray burns it up; but if it has sap, the sun’s ray warms it, causing it to grow. It is the same in the life of the **Essence** <note>original: "Essenz"; the underlying spiritual substance of a person.</note> in man: if that life does not have the **Ens** <note>term: "Ens" (Latin for 'being' or 'essence'); here it refers to the spiritual "fuel" or "matter" derived from God's nature.</note> of God’s gentleness and love—as if from the **eternal One**—then it hardens itself into a fierce, fiery sharpness. The **mind** <note>original: "Gemüth"; the inner seat of emotions and will.</note> then becomes entirely rough, hungry, greedy, envious, and prickly. Such a false sense and will then passes from the inner life into the body, and into all the person's being and works.

26. Thus, such a fiery, greedy, envious nature destroys everything good with the sharp **sense** <note>original: "Sensu"</note> of its life. There is danger in everything it touches, for it injects its venomous rays into it, seeking to pull everything to itself and infect it with its poison, like a hungry greed. But if it happens that the fiery life can eat of Divine Love, it becomes like a light that breaks forth and goes out from a fire. In this way, the true life breaks out from the fiery nature with a new spirit and a will of Divine Love from within; it is no longer "taking," as is the nature of fire, but "giving." For the will of love gives itself, just as light gives itself from the fire, flowing into all things and working good in everything.

### Chapter 3. VI. On Divine **Contemplation** <term>Beschauligkeit</term>.

The Word was with God, and God was the Word; the same was in the beginning with God. All things are made through the same; and without the same, nothing is made that is made. <note>John 1:1-3. The author uses this biblical foundation to explain the transition from an undifferentiated Godhead to the physical universe.</note>

1. The beginning of all beings was the **Word**, as the breathing out of God, and God was the eternal **One** from eternity, and remains so for eternity. But the Word is the emanation <note>original: "Ausfluß"; literally an "outflowing." This describes how God projects his inner essence outward to create the world.</note> of the Divine Will or the Divine Knowledge. Just as the senses flow out from the mind, and yet the mind is only **One**; so too was the eternal **One** within the emanation of the Will. This means: In the beginning was the **WORD**; for the Word, as the emanation from the Will of God, was the eternal beginning, and remains so eternally. For it is the revelation of the eternal **One**, through which the Divine Power is brought into a conscious knowledge of "Something"; and by the **WORD**, we understand the revealed Will of God, and by the word **GOD**, we understand the hidden God as the eternal **One**, from which the Word eternally arises.

2. Thus the emanation of the Divine **One** is the **WORD**, and yet it is God Himself, as His own revelation.

3. This emanation flows out from God, and that which has flowed out is Wisdom—the beginning and cause of all powers, colors, virtues, and properties.

4. From such a revelation of powers, in which the Will of the eternal **One** contemplates itself, there flows out the understanding and the knowledge of the Something <term>Ichts</term> <note>A term coined by Böhme to describe the transition from "Nothing" (the undifferentiated Godhead) to "Something" (manifested reality). It is the opposite of "Nichts" (Nothing).</note>, where the eternal Will beholds itself in the "Something," and leads into a delight within Wisdom toward a likeness and image.

5. And this same image is the *Great Mystery* <note>original Latin: "Mysterium Magnum." In this context, it refers to the spiritual "womb" or "chaos" from which all matter and life are differentiated.</note>, as the Creator of all beings and creatures; for it is the *Separator* <note>original Latin: "Separator"; the active principle that divides, distinguishes, and organizes the undifferentiated divine essence into specific forms.</note> within the emanation of the Will, which makes the Will of the eternal **One** divisible: It is the divisibility within the Will, from which powers and properties originate.

6. These same powers are in turn an emanation of themselves, where each power leads into its own will according to the virtue of that same power: from this, the plurality of wills originates...

This is the softening and joy of the coarse, painful spirit of sulfur and salt. 22. The third spirit is the **tincture** <term>Tinctur</term> <note>In Böhme’s theosophy, the Tincture is the highest, most refined spiritual principle that "colors" or transforms matter, bringing it closer to the divine state.</note>, acting as a counter-reflection <term>Gegenwurf</term> of the divine **great mystery** <term>Mysterii Magni</term> <note>Latin: "Mysterium Magnum"; the primordial "chaos" or treasury of all potential that exists before creation.</note>, wherein all powers reside in equality. It is rightly called Paradise or Divine Delight: it is a housing of divine power, a housing of the eternal souls, from which all external powers spring, in the same way that air springs from fire.

It works with the visible elements of the body and shows itself outwardly, so that one understands that God’s Spirit works together in the labor of faith, just as He works with and through the power of the elemental world, making Himself visible through the essence of this world as a counter-image <note>original: *Gegenwurf*; Böhme uses this term to describe how the spiritual world projects itself or reflects into a material form.</note>.

Thus, everything I look upon, be it evil or good, I can truly say: here, in this thing, the hidden spirit of the **Separator** <term>Separatoris</term> <note>original Latin: *separatoris*; in Böhme’s thought, the "Separator" is the divine power that differentiates the primordial unity into various specific qualities and forms.</note> of all beings has formed itself into a specific quality. Here, it has made for itself a counter-image or likeness according to its outflowing, whether toward evil or good—all according to the properties of nature, such as heat or cold, harshness, bitterness, sweetness or sourness. In all such formation, there is only such an elemental nature on the outside, like a specific sulfur and salt; but in the inward ground, in the **Tincture** <term>Tinctur</term> <note>The spiritual "essence" or life-force that gives a thing its true quality.</note>, it is good and useful, and belongs to its own likeness, for the **Nourishment** <term>Nutrimento</term> <note>original Latin: *nutrimento*; referring to the spiritual and physical sustenance of life.</note> of life, which stands according to the **Astral** <term>Astralischen</term> <note>Relating to the influence of the stars or the "sidereal" spirit that bridges the physical and divine.</note> and **Elemental** <term>Elementischen</term> nature, in all qualities, according to its external ground.

34. Every single thing—be it herb, grass, trees, animal, birds, fish, worms, or whatever it may be—is useful and has come forth from the **Separator** of all beings, as from the **WORD** or the distinguishing will of **GOD**. Through this, the **Separator** has made a likeness or image of each thing’s quality, in which he works.

35. For this visible world, with all its host and essence, is nothing other than a counter-image of the spiritual world, which is hidden within this material, elemental world, just as the **Tincture** is hidden in herbs and metals.

36. And just as the Tincture <term>Tinctur</term> <note>In Böhme’s thought, the "Tincture" is the hidden, vitalizing spiritual essence that gives life, color, and virtue to the physical world.</note> forms itself and makes itself visible through its virtue in all things and through its outflow, so that one can see and recognize by the figure (as well as by the colors and smell) what kind of Separator <note>original Latin: *Separator*; the divine agent that differentiates the primordial unity into specific forms.</note> or outflow of the Divine Will has flowed forth from the Great Mystery <note>original Latin: *Mysterio Magno*; the "Great Mystery" is the hidden potentiality or "chaos" of God from which all creation emerges.</note>: so too can one recognize the inner ground from which the visible world—the sun, stars, elements, and all creatures—has sprung.

37. For no thing or essence of a thing has come to its place from afar, but rather its ground is in the very place where it grows. The elements have their cause within themselves, from which they spring; likewise, the stars have their chaos <note>In this context, "chaos" refers to the primordial source or raw spiritual material.</note> within themselves, in which they stand.

38. The elements are nothing other than a pictorial, moving essence of the invisible, unmoving one.

39. Likewise, the stars are an outflow of the properties of the Spiritual World, according to the differentiation of the Separator <note>original: *Separatoris*</note>, the ground of which is the **WORD**, or the differentiable Will of **GOD**.

40. The essence and weaving of the elements is fire, air, water, and earth (wherein there is thick and thin, wet and dry, hard and soft); these are composed into one essence. It is not that each has a separate origin and lineage, but they all come only from a single ground, and that same place from which they have come is everywhere. One need only consider how, in one place, a greater ignition according to a certain property has occurred than in another, whereby the movement became greater, and the matter in such form and essence became more abundant than in another; this can be understood in the matter of the earth, as well as in the water and air, just as there is a difference at each pole <note>original: *Polo*; referring to geographical or spiritual orientations.</note> as in every place upon the earth. From this also arises the difference in customs and virtues, as well as in the regimes, order, and creatures.

41. Furthermore, the division of such properties has all arisen from the Great Mystery <note>original: *Mysterio Magno*</note> through the one-time movement of the powers of all beings, just as the Single Will of all beings moved itself at once, and out of the Infin—

41. ...sensitivity into sensitivity and the distinctness of the powers, and made the eternal power active and willing, so that in every power a counter-reflection <term>Gegenwurf</term> <note>The *Gegenwurf* is a central concept in Böhme's thought, referring to a "counter-throw" or a mirror-like reflection that allows a power to become conscious of itself.</note> arose as its own desire. This same desire, within the counter-reflection of the powers, has again projected itself into a further counter-reflection; from this, the desire of such an outflow became sharp, harsh, and coarse, and has coagulated <term>coaguliret</term> <note>To "coagulate" here means the transition from a purely spiritual or energetic state into a solid, material state.</note> and turned into material substances.

42. And just as the outflow of the inner powers originated from light and darkness, from sharpness and gentleness, from a fiery or a light-like nature: so too did the material substances become. The further the outflow of a power stretched, the more external and coarse the matter became; for one counter-reflection proceeded from another, until finally reaching the coarse earth.

43. We must, however, fully complete and indicate the basis of such philosophy <term>Philosophiæ</term>—how hard and soft took their origin—which we recognize in the metals. For every substance that is hard, such as metals and stones, as well as wood, herbs, and the like, contains within itself a very noble tincture <term>Tinctur</term> and a high spirit of power. This can also be seen in the bones of creatures: the noblest tincture according to the power of the light, as the greatest sweetness, lies in the marrow of the bones; whereas in the blood there lies only a fiery tincture, as in sulfur <term>Schwefel</term>, salt <term>Salz</term>, and mercury <term>Mercurio</term> <note>These three—Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury—were considered by 17th-century alchemists to be the "tria prima," the three primary components of all physical matter.</note>. This is understood as follows:

44. **GOD** is the eternal One, the greatest gentleness, insofar as He is within Himself apart from His movement and revelation; but His movement—in that He is called one **God** in Trinity <term>Dreyfaltigkeit</term>, as a Triune Being where one speaks of Three and yet only of One, and where He is called the Eternal Power and Word—this is the precious and highest ground. One must contemplate how the Divine Will encloses itself in a place of selfhood, as a power, and works within itself, yet goes out through its working and makes for itself a counter-reflection, which is Wisdom <term>Weisheit</term> <note>In Böhme’s mysticism, Wisdom (Sophia) is the divine mirror or "looking-glass" through which the unmanifest God views His own possibilities and brings them into creation.</note>, through which the ground and origin of all beings has sprung.

45. Likewise, know this: everything in the essence of this world that is soft, gentle, and thin is out-flowing and self-giving. Its ground and origin is according to the Unity <note>original: *Einheit*; the primal, undifferentiated state of God.</note> of eternity, as the Unity always flows out from itself. This is why in the essence of "thinness"—such as water and air—one perceives no sensitivity or pain, for that essence is unified within itself.

46. But that which is hard and compressing—such as bones, wood, herbs, metals, fire, earth, stones, and similar materials—within them lies the image of Divine Power and Motion. It encloses itself with its *Separator* <note>original: *Separatore*; the force that distinguishes and manifests specific qualities from the primal source.</note> (as the outflow of Divine Desire), like a noble jewel or spark of Divine Power, protected from coarseness. It is hard and fiery because it has its ground in the Divine In-dwelling <term>Insaßlichkeit</term> <note>The state of being "seated" or fixed within a foundation; the localized presence of the divine within a specific form.</note>; for the Eternal One always introduces itself into a ground of the Trinity to set the powers in motion, yet it closes itself off from the outflow—the introduction of Nature’s own will—and works with the power of Unity through Nature.

47. This is also how the noble tincture <term>Tinktur</term> <note>In alchemy and Böhme's thought, the 'tincture' is the hidden spiritual essence or 'dye' that gives life and quality to matter.</note> is to be understood. Where it is most noble, it is most firmly enclosed by hardness. For the Unity lies within it in a state of mobility, as a sensitivity of action, and therefore it hides itself. But in "thinness" <note>referring to fluid or airy substances</note> it does not lie in such sensitivity but is equal to all things—just as water and air are equal to all things and are in all things. However, the "dry water" is the true pearl-ground <term>Perlen-Grund</term> <note>A metaphorical term for the matrix or source of spiritual wisdom and the 'pearl of great price.'</note>, wherein the subtle power of the Unity's working lies in the *Center* <note>original: *Centro*</note>. To those of our own who are worthy of this, it is hereby indicated: do not busy yourselves seeking the mystery in soft things that lack a fiery nature. Thus, understand this mystery:

### VI. On Divine Contemplation. Chap. 3. 198

...balance <term>Temperamentum</term> <note>original: *Temperamentum*; the state of perfect balance where all conflicting qualities are harmonized into one.</note>, wherein lies the distinctness <note>original: *Schiedlichkeit*; the state of being differentiated yet still part of a whole.</note> of all powers. 49. The spirits of strong power in the odor must be brought into balance—into Unity—and not allowed to fly away. Otherwise, when one tries to cure with salt, as if with the sharpness of fire, one gives the patient the "soul" without the "spirit."

50. The soul of such balsams is divided in its properties; each one expresses itself separately in its own great joy, but in their separation they are too rebellious. They do not unify the life's enmity and division, but rather ignite the division of life even more.

51. Enclose them and make them one, so that they all have one Will in love; then you have the "little pearl" <note>A recurring metaphor in Böhme's work for the hidden spark of divine wisdom or the "Philosopher's Stone."</note> of the whole world. To provoke to anger creates pride and strife, which can be recognized in all things.

52. A prisoner is only comforted by his release; he places his will in hope and composes himself with patience, until finally his restlessness falls through hope into the balance of the temperament, and in such hope he learns to become humble. When he is then told of his release, he rejoices.

53. So also you physicians, take note: this is your pearl, if you are able to understand this; the meaning is both inward and outward.

## CONVERSATION OF AN ENLIGHTENED AND A TO-BE-ENLIGHTENED SOUL,
<note>Original Latin title: *Colloquium Animæ Illuminatæ et Illuminandæ*.</note>
### or Dialogue between an enlightened and an unenlightened soul.

->Summaries.<-

A poor soul had turned away from God toward the creature <note>In this context, "the creature" refers to the material world and created things rather than the Creator.</note>, § 1–9. It worshipped the devil within its own self-will, 10–12; lived in wrath, 13, and evil desires, 14, toward pride and power, 15, greed and self-centered anxiety; 16. whereby its life became dark and the powers of God were lost. 17. Then envy and enmity awoke, 18, as did wrath and murder, 19, which is hell or the wrath of God, with the extinguishing of Divine Love. 20. The devil’s impulse plunged the soul into every vice, 21, and its blindness was so great that it did not recognize the devil. 22. As the soul ran on in such a way of life, the call of Christ reached it. 23. Then it saw its own monstrous form, 24, 25, and turned in earnest toward God. 26. Conflict then arose from within and without; 27. the devil confuses the good senses, 28, and hinders prayer; 29. at which the soul is terrified, 30, and raises itself more vehemently in prayer to God. 31. Nevertheless, the devil awakens earthly desire, 32, and hinders prayer; 33. he speaks lies, 34, and presents the vanity of the world and Christ's merit <note>The devil here uses "Christ's merit" as a false comfort to suggest the soul doesn't need to change its behavior.</note>—suggesting that one should not make a fool of oneself, but should rather collect money first, <term>etc.</term> <note>Original: *zc.*, an abbreviation for *et cetera*.</note> 36. From this, great unrest arises in the soul, 37, so that it seeks all kinds of ways to find rest and obtain God’s grace; 38. but it cannot find it, 39, for it is blind to Christ. 40. However, it meets a true Christian, 41, to whom it reveals its condition; 42. the Christian gives the soul a good account; 43. at which the soul is terrified and becomes faint-hearted, 44, and begins to wrestle with doubt. 45. The Christian further instructs the soul, 46, 47, and teaches it how it should conduct itself, 48, so that the Love of God might meet it; 49. 50. teaching it to leave the world and perform good works; 51. not to oppress the wretched, whose sighing awakens God's wrath in the oppressor of the poor; 52. 53. and how it should further abandon the "beasts" <note>Metaphors for various sins or earthly passions.</note> of its evil inclinations so that they may die within it, 54, even though this path of <term>dying to the self</term> <note>Original: *Absterbung*, a mystical term for the process where the ego's worldly desires are put to death.</note> is very narrow and full of anxiety. 55. Therefore, the soul should live in Christ, 56, whose kingdom is not of this world, 57, and follow Him in self-denial, 58, leaving all earthly things behind.

<header>VII. Conversation of an Enlightened [Soul]</header>

1. A poor soul had wandered out of Paradise and had come into the kingdom of this world; there the devil met her and spoke to her: Where are you going, you half-blind soul?

2. The soul spoke: I want to behold the creatures <note>The "creatures" refers to all created things in the material world.</note> of the world which the Creator has made.

3. The devil spoke: How do you wish to behold them, since you cannot recognize them, or from what essence and property they are? You see them only as a painted image and cannot truly know them.

4. The soul spoke: How might I then know them in their essence and being?

5. The devil spoke: If you eat of that from which the creatures are made, both Good and Evil, then your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God Himself and recognize what the Creator is.

6. The soul spoke: I am noble and holy, and I might die from that, as the Creator has spoken.

7. The devil spoke: You shall by no means die, but your eyes will be opened, and you will be just as God is, and will know Evil and Good: moreover, you will become powerful, mighty, and great, as I am; all the wit <note>In this context, "wit" (Witze) refers to the inner wisdom, logic, or governing principles of created things.</note> of the creatures will be revealed to you.

### VII. Conversation of an Enlightened [Soul]

22. The soul did as the devil advised, yet she did not recognize him as the devil; instead, she thought it was her own cleverness and understanding, and that she was doing well and right.

23. As she thus lived in such a manner, our dear **Lord Jesus Christ** met her at a certain time with **God's** love and wrath. He had come into this world to destroy the works of the devil and to pass judgment over all ungodly works. With a mighty power, He spoke into her through His suffering, dying, and death, shattering the devil’s works within her. He opened the way to His grace, looked upon her with His mercy, and called her back, saying she should turn away and repent; then He would redeem her from such a mask-like form <note>original: "Larven=Bildniß." In Jacob Böhme’s mystical language, a "larva" or "mask" refers to the distorted, monstrous outward appearance the soul takes on when it falls away from God’s light into the "dark world."</note> and lead her back into Paradise.

24. When this happened, and the spark of Divine Light became manifest within her, she looked at herself along with her works and her will. She became aware that she stood in Hell within **God's** wrath, and recognized that she was a mask and a monster before **God** and the Kingdom of Heaven. At this she was so greatly terrified that the greatest anguish awoke within her, for the judgment of **God** was made manifest in her.

25. When this occurred, the **Lord Christ** spoke into her with His voice of grace: Repent and leave vanity behind, and you shall come to my grace.

26. The soul, in her mask-like form and with the soiled robe of vanity, stepped before **God** and prayed for grace, that **God** would forgive her sins; she firmly visualized the satisfaction and reconciliation of our **Lord Jesus Christ**.

27. But the evil properties of the serpents formed in the Astral Spirit <term>Astral Spirit</term> <note>In this context, the Astral Spirit refers to the part of the human psyche influenced by the physical stars and the elements of the world. Instead, they brought their own lusts and desires into it, for they did not want to die to their own pleasure or leave the world, as they were *of* the world; they also feared the world's mockery if they were to leave behind their worldly honor and glory. But the poor soul turned her face toward **God** and desired grace from Him, that **God** would give her His love.

# VII. Dialogue of an Enlightened [Soul]
## Page 210
<meta>catchword: captive</meta>

...[fir]st attack of grace, and she did not know it, that Christ was standing in her hells <note>Böhme often refers to "hells" in the plural to describe the various internal states of torment and separation from God within the human soul.</note> amidst God's wrath and strict justice, and was fighting with the embodied Satan and spirit of error in soul and body. 41. By God’s providence, this poor, troubled soul once encountered a soul enlightened and reborn by God, who spoke to her: "What is the matter with you, you troubled soul, that you are so restless and stand in such sorrow?"

42. ### VII. Dialogue of an Enlightened Soul

[...you should] envision the **Lord Jesus Christ** most firmly, and immerse all your reason and senses into Him; you must desire to remain in Him forever, and desire to die to your creatures within Him.

59. Furthermore, you must most firmly resolve <note>original: "einbilden." In Böhme's terminology, this refers to "imagination" not as fantasy, but as the soul's power to form itself into a specific spiritual image or state.</note> to turn your pleasure and mind away from all false complacency, and not allow yourself to be held by temporal honor and goods; you must also put away from yourself whatever is unjust and may hinder you. Your will must be entirely pure, and directed toward such an earnest purpose that you never again wish to enter into your false creaturely self, but rather leave it at that very hour, and separate your mind from it; also, you must desire at that very hour to step onto the pure way of truth and righteousness, and follow the teaching of Christ.

60. And just as you now intend to leave the enemies of your own nature, so must you yourself also forgive all your external enemies, and intend to meet them with your love, so that there may be no creature <term>Creature: Here refers to an attachment or obsession with another person or thing that "captures" the soul's attention and prevents it from turning fully to God.</term> that might seize your will and hold you back, but that it may become pure of every creature.

61. Also, you must be willing to gladly leave all your temporal honor and goods for Christ's sake, if it should be so, and you must not wish to take up anything that is earthly to love it. Instead, you should regard yourself in your station and temporal honors and goods only as a servant of **God** and of your fellow Christians—as a steward <term>Haushalter: A manager of property belonging to another. Böhme suggests that one can possess wealth only if they treat it as God's property, managed for the benefit of others.</term> of **God** in your office. The "high eyes" of self-love must be broken and humbled, so that no creatures remain within which lead the senses into false images.

62. Furthermore, you must firmly envision that you will certainly obtain the promised grace in the merit of **Jesus Christ**, as His overflowing love, which will redeem you from those creatures, and enlighten your will, and kindle it with the flame of love, through which you become victorious against the devil.

# VII. Dialogue of an Enlightened Soul

74. Then the **Blasphemer** <note>original: *Låsterer*. This refers to the Accuser or the Devil, who attempts to undermine the soul's spiritual progress through doubt.</note> approached her, wanting to invalidate her path and lead her into doubt, and whispered to her: "It is not from **God**; it was only your imagination."

75. Then the **Divine Light** receded from her and glowed only in the innermost depths like a **smoldering fire** <note>original: *Moder-Feuer*. This describes a fire that burns low without a flame, like embers under ash, representing a state where faith remains but the joy of "light" is hidden.</note>, so that **Reason** <note>original: *Vernunft*. In Böhme’s writing, Reason is often personified as the worldly, logical mind that struggles to grasp spiritual mysteries.</note> saw herself as completely foolish and abandoned. She did not know what was happening to her, or if it were truly certain that she had tasted the divine light of grace—yet she could not let go of it.

76. For the fire-burning love of **God** had been sown within her, through which a great hunger and thirst for divine sweetness arose. Now she truly began to pray, to humble herself before **God**, to examine her evil **inclinations** <note>original: *Neiglichkeit*. This refers to the innate human tendency toward worldly desires or sin.</note> in her thoughts, and to reject them.

77. By this, the will of **Reason** was broken, and the evil, innate inclination was killed more and more. This caused great pain to the nature of the body, which fell into a faint, like a sickness; yet it was not a natural sickness, but rather a **melancholy** <note>original: *Melancholia*. To 17th-century readers, this was a physical and spiritual state of heaviness; here, it results from the body being denied its usual "false" worldly pleasures.</note> of the earthly nature of the body, because its false desires were being broken.

78. Now, as earthly **Reason** found herself so forsaken, and the poor soul saw that she was mocked from the outside by the scorn of the world—because she no longer wished to walk in the godless way—and was also attacked from within by the **Blasphemer** (who mocked her and constantly held up the world's wealth, beauty, and glory before her, judging her to be foolish in comparison), she thought: "O eternal **God**, what must You do now so that You may come to rest?"

### Concerning the causes of fear or sadness, and what constitutes horror or anxiety.

->Summary Points.<-

All fear and sadness come from the soul, §. 1. because it is held in a dark dungeon by the spirit of this world. *ibid.* This has four lodgings, 2. namely the *choleric*, 3. *sanguine*, 4. *phlegmatic*, 5. and *melancholic*, 6-8. In one of these housings the soul lies captive, 9. and one dwells within the other. 10. The soul is a *magical* fire-source <note>original: "Feuer-Quall," an archaic term for a well-spring or bubbling source of energy</note> from the nature of God the Father, a great longing for the Light; 11. its root is the dark world, 12. it desires spiritual essence, 13. and turned itself outward in Adam, 14. it eats in the mother's womb from the *Spirit of the World*, <note>original: "Spiritu Mundi," the vital breath or astrological influence that animates the physical world</note> 15. and must have the <term>Complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—choleric, sanguine, phlegmatic, and melancholic—which were thought to determine a person's temperament and physical health.</note> or power for its food. 16. From this comes the distinction of humans in their will and actions, 17. and the constant struggle between the soul and the <term>complexion</term>, 18. where the love of God often triumphs when the soul eats from the essence of God's love; 19. but where it eats from the <term>complexion</term>, it performs the will of the stars, 20. and here one sees what sin is. 21. God's Spirit does not enter into the fire. 22.

All sadness and fear, where a person is horrified and afraid within themselves, comes from the soul. For the external spirit from the stars and the elements <note>The physical components of the world</note> is not horrified, since it lives in its mother who gave birth to it; but the poor soul has entered into a foreign lodging with Adam, namely into the spirit of this world; there the beautiful creature <note>referring to the soul as a created being</note> is covered up and held in a dark dungeon.

2. The spirit of this world has four lodgings <note>original: "Herbergen," meaning inns or dwellings</note> in which the noble jewel <note>A common metaphor in this period for the soul or the divine spark within man.</note> stands locked away. Among these four, usually one—and not all four—is primarily manifest in a person, according to the four elements that every person has within themselves. The person is that very essence, with the exception of the soul, which is not that same essence but lies imprisoned within it. Yet only one lodging or form among the four holds the supreme rule over life. These four are called (1) Choleric, (2) Sanguine, (3) Phlegmatic, and (4) Melancholic.

3. (1) **Choleric** is of the nature and property of fire; it gives strong courage, sudden anger, the rising of pride, stubbornness, and a disregard for others. This form shines according to the outer world in a fire-light; it works according to the power of the sun and always desires to be the master.

4. (2) **Sanguine**, according to the air, is subtle, friendly, and cheerful, yet not of strong courage. It is changeable and easily moved from one thing to another. It naturally receives the properties and wit of the stars in its essence; it is modest and pure, and carries great secrets in its knowledge.

5. (3) **Phlegmatic** is according to the nature and property of water; it is fleshy, coarse, and soft, of a womanly <note>In the historical context of the four humors, "womanly" was often used to describe qualities considered passive or receptive rather than active.</note> will and moderate understanding. However, it holds fast to what it receives. Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to skill, knowledge, or craft.</note> must be brought into it through sound and teaching; it does not invent it from its own root. It lets everything be as it is and does not fall into melancholy; it has a shimmer of light, being neither sad nor highly joyful, but treats everything as easy and common.

6. (4) **Melancholic** is of the nature and property of the earth; like the earth, it is cold, rigid, dark, sad, and hungry for the light, always fearful of God’s wrath.

7. For the earth and stones are outside the eternal essence; that is, they were seized in the ignited desire in the <term>Fiat</term> <note>A Latin term meaning "let it be," referring to the divine command of creation.</note> according to the property of wrath as well as love; it is a mixture of evil and good. The good always has a fear of the evil; there is a constant fleeing—the good always wants to flee from the evil, as can be seen in metal, where its <term>tincture</term> <note>In alchemy and Boehme’s philosophy, the "tincture" is the hidden, spiritual essence or "soul" of a substance that gives it its color and virtues.</note> is good, while the entirely earthly part is evil and fierce. There, the tincture of the metals always wants to flee from the earthly,

Therefore, Christ became a human in our essence so that He might turn the soul back through the Center and through the fire of God into the light—that is, into the world of gentleness <term>Gentleness: In Böhme's thought, "Sanftmuth" (meekness/gentleness) is the quality of the Light-World that tempers the harsh "fire" of the soul.</term>—which has now occurred in the person of Christ.

It is the soul’s kindling; the complexion becomes soul-like within the soul’s fire. It must eat from one of these, or it would perish; yet no perishing is possible for it, for it is a desire. Now, where there is a desire, there is also essence; the desire creates its own essence.

17. Now we understand why there is such a difference among humans in their will and actions. For whatever the soul eats, in which its fire-life is kindled, that is what governs the soul's life. 18. The soul struggles against the temperament, for they are now bound together. The temperament struggles against the soul; it always wants to enter the **Soul-fire** and ignite itself so that it might truly live. For when the soul eats of God’s Word, the temperament becomes faint and as if imprisoned in relation to the outward life, even though it still lives within itself.

19. Yet the soul is so faithful—before God's love, which alone comes to the aid of its essence—that it often (when it eats of God’s love-essence) brings a triumph and a Divine taste into the temperament. From this, the temperament becomes trembling and highly joyful, awakening the whole body as if Paradise were now present. However, this does not always last; the soul is soon covered by something else (which falls into the temperament and introduces the external imagination from the spirit of the great world into the temperament), from which it receives a mirror and begins to project its imagination into it. Thus, it departs from the Spirit of God and is often wallowed in the mud, unless the **Virgin of Divine Wisdom** <note>original: "Jungfrau Göttlicher Weisheit." Also known as Sophia, she represents the divine mirror or the feminine principle of God’s wisdom that calls the soul back to its source.</note> calls it to turn back again, she who is set before the soul as a mirror.

### 1. The Choleric Temperament <term>Complexion: From the Latin *complexio*, the four humors or temperaments (choleric, sanguine, phlegmatic, melancholic) believed to govern human nature.</term> according to the Element of Fire.

23. If the soul-life is surrounded by the **Choleric Temperament**, it is fiery, fierce, rising, and consuming; it also produces a body that is lean, malicious, fierce, and angry. And when the soul projects its imagination into it, it ignites the temperament even more severely, for the soul is also fiery. Then there arises in the human being: anger, pride, a desire to rise up in power and splendor, to suppress everything beneath oneself, to be a mocker of the wretched, a ruler over bowed knees, caring nothing if someone dies in their rage—unless the stars <note>The "stars" refer to the astrological and external cosmic influences that Böhme believed shaped a person's earthly fate and personality.</note> prevent it, which often happens through a combination of temperaments that creates obstacles and prevents much.

24. There is great danger in this temperament when the soul lives in external imagination; it has a hard bond when one fiery-torment is bound to another.

25. The fierce Devil has a powerful access to it, for the property of Fire serves him. He is also proud and envious, and so is this temperament. Oh, how difficult it is for the soul to get free when it is truly ignited in this property! The Devil does not even need to tempt it; it follows him quite willingly to his own tune <note>original: "nach seiner Geigen," literally "to his fiddle." An idiom meaning to do exactly as someone else wishes.</note>. It does not easily become sad, for it possesses a **fire-light** within the temperament, and it always thinks it is God's light and that it is on a good path; yet it is a proud, envious, angry, powerful, and oppressive will and spirit, as long as the soul relies solely on the temperament. Oh, it loves to give off a glittering appearance in its splendor, out of its fiery temperament and luster; in its great pride and arrogance, it even wants to be praised as holy. Oh, you Devil in an angel's form, how dark you will be when the temperament breaks apart in death!

### 2. The Sanguine Temperament according to the Element of Air.

26. The **Sanguine Temperament** is gentle, light, and full of joy, according to the property of the Air; it is sensual, gentle, and lovely, and resembles life itself.

27. If the soul is surrounded by this temperament and projects its imagination into it, wishing to live within it, the soul shows itself to be friendly and cunning; it wishes to experience much, and much comes readily to its hand.

The soul experiences everything the stars do within this temperament. It is joyful, yet soon discouraged by the power of fire (as if before the "big shots" <note>original: "grossen Hansen," a German idiom for powerful, arrogant, or influential people.</note>), but within itself, it is powerful in its own mind, without needing counsel. It possesses sharp reason through the temperament according to the external spirit; it does not easily do anything harmful in anger and is at times uplifting and magnanimous, yet at other times falling again, just like the air. It must be on guard, for the Devil is hostile toward it; he cannot do much to it within this temperament, so he would like to confuse it so that it might harbor many different senses, preventing it from imagining <note>In Böhme’s writing, "imagination" is a technical term for the soul's ability to focus its desire and "form" its inner reality toward either God or the world.</note> toward the Kingdom of God. He throws strange things before it to pass its time; it enjoys studying many things, for the stars throw their imagination into the air, from which the soul receives many strange, rambling thoughts.

28. Such a person leads a weak, common, pious, and simple life, shared with everyone; but the Devil excellently goads his enemies against him. He must suffer much but passes through it easily, just as air passes through something. He is rarely very sad, for he does not carry a fiery heart, and so terror does not burn harshly within him. Yet he should guard against unchastity and idolatry, for in these things the Devil gains access to the temperament.

### 3. The Phlegmatic Temperament according to the Element of Water.

29. If the soul is surrounded by this temperament and blows its life out from it, it is a thick, swollen life—clumsy, almost base and easily disregarded, with a coarse body and poor reason. Yet, through teaching, all common matters can be brought into it. If the power of the Moon <note>Böhme associates the Moon with the element of Water and the Phlegmatic temperament, representing a reflective, changeable, and sometimes dull influence.</note> does not assist it, it is quite a coarse block—and furthermore, almost unjust through the Moon's power.

30. One can carve all sorts of things out of this temperament; the water-spirit accepts everything, sometimes evil, sometimes good. It gladly presents itself as a holy hypocrite and attributes a pious, just life to itself, but it is all mixed together. Water is deceptive in appearance; the soul does not easily perceive God’s wrath or the dark world (which is in its center). It bites greedily at the abominations of the world and hides them under the appearance of water, thinking it to be the radiance of God.
