31. The Devil can introduce all vices (which he knows in hell) into this <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "Complexion." In the 17th century, this referred to the balance of bodily humors and the spiritual disposition they created.</note>, provided the stars do not prevent it and the soul permits it. Here he gains as much as he does in fire—the fiery temperament—for sin is regarded as lightly within it as a stream of water flows along. He also has the power to plague the soul with sadness here if it tries to escape him. For he darkens the luster of the water with the sins he has introduced and hedges in the soul so that it remains held back from GOD. But in the storm of the soul, if it tries to run away from him with force out of the "house of mourning," he cannot hold his ground here; the temperament is too weak, whereas he can hold on better in the fire.

### 4. The Melancholic Temperament according to the Earth.

32. The Melancholic temperament resembles the sorrowful earth, which stands always in fear before the <term>wrath of God</term> <note>original: "Grimm GOttes." In Böhme's theology, the "Grimm" or "Fierceness" is the harsh, dark quality of nature that exists apart from God's light.</note> that entered into it during the creation. It gives a moderate understanding, yet one that is somewhat deep-thinking and meditative.

33. The chamber of this temperament stands open; much may be grasped within it, provided that <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "Schwermuth," literally "heaviness of spirit."</note> does not hinder it. If the soul is surrounded by this temperament so that it "eats" from it, its fire-burning becomes almost dark and very sad. It does not think much of worldly luxury; through the temperament, it is always heavy-hearted and fearful like the earth. The Devil attacks it hard, for he would always like to plunge it completely into darkness, into his own kingdom.

34. For where it is dark, there he gladly enters; he creates <term>phantoms</term> <note>original: "Fürbilde," meaning mental images or simulacra used to deceive.</note> for the soul and terrifies it with his malice so that it might despair of God's grace. For otherwise, the soul in this chamber of melancholy does not bring much that is useful to him—unless it should become reckless regarding God’s grace and turn entirely frivolous. In that case, the body can produce a murderer and a robber who regards man, God, and the Devil all as equal. For if the soul becomes reckless and gives itself over to whatever the temperament does with it, then this person does everything that the stars work within the temperament, and the Devil mixes his <term>imagination</term> <note>Böhme uses "Imagination" to describe the soul's power to focus its desire and give "form" to its inner reality.</note> into it.

35. But because it remains in conflict against the sorrowful temperament, there is none among these four temperaments where fewer...

37. In no <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "Complexion." In the 17th century, this referred to the "four humors" that were thought to govern human health and personality.</note> is the Devil’s will more clearly revealed (if the soul is kindled in God's light and love) than in the Melancholic one, as those who are spiritually afflicted know well when they shatter his robber-castle. 38. Oh, how deceitfully he deals with the soul, just as a fowler stalks birds! He terrifies it during prayer (especially at night, when it is dark), casting his <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Imagination." He constantly acts as if he had power over the soul, as if it were his own, yet he has not the power of a single hair over it, unless the soul itself despairs and gives itself up to him. He is not permitted to touch or possess the soul spiritually; he only shoots his imagination into it through the temperament.

39. This is the reason why he attacks the soul so: because the chamber of the temperament is dark. He cannot slide his imagination into the light; he can only do so through the sins of man. However, in this temperament, he can do it because it is close to his own desire, since this desire creates darkness and fear because of the "rough earth." Otherwise, he has not a spark more right within or to this temperament than any other. He can accomplish nothing more with his imagination than to terrify the person and make them timid...

40. The soul has free will; if it stands before the Devil and does not will as he wills, he does not have enough power to even touch the outer, sinful body. 42. But if he brings the soul to the point that it consents to do such things for him, then he is like the executioner who binds a prisoner and leads him to judgment: yet even then, he is not permitted to judge or cast the soul down, unless it does so itself.

### Recipe for the Black Devil.

->Summaries<-

The Devil must be mocked. §. 43. One must not dispute with him, 44. nor pay him any mind, 45. but rather hold God’s promises before him. 46. 47. Fear comes from the Devil's imagination. 48. He comes only with terrors, 53. therefore do not yield to him, 54. for he does not easily frighten a defiant person. 55. 56. Christ is yours, do not let Him go, 60. He does not forget the soul, 61. 62. therefore no one should doubt His grace. 63.

43. When he attacks the poor soul, trying to make it despair, one should (when he comes) give him this **prescription**<note>original: "Recept." Böhme uses the word in the sense of a medical prescription or recipe to "cure" the Devil's presence.</note> to eat: the Devil is a proud, haughty spirit, and one can do him no greater pain—making him retreat more quickly—than to take fresh courage against him. Be quite defiant and high-spirited; do not be terrified by him (for he has not the power of a single straw) and only mock him. Reproach him with his own fall: how he was once such a beautiful angel and has now become a black devil.

44. At first, give him no answer; rather, when he comes and strikes at the soul through the imagination, throwing evil thoughts into you and reproaching you with your sins—acting as if he wants to carry you away in a terrifying vision—then take a defiant courage against him, saying:

45. "Look at that! From where have you come, **Black Hans**?<note>original: "Schwarz-Hans." everything. How have you, once a beautiful angel, become a carrier of the **sack of sins**? From a prince to a **beadle-servant**? <note>A "beadle-servant" (Büttel-Knecht) was a low-ranking officer or bailiff who carried out arrests and punishments. Devour that as well, and you might become an angel again!

52. Do not let your senses dispute with him, and do not be terrified of him. Simply make yourself bold, whether by day or night. He dare not do anything to you if you mock him in the most gruesome way when he gives you cause; otherwise, do not mock him.

53. If he does not come with a terror of fear, then he is not there; rather, it is the soul’s own recoiling before the dark abyss, which is terrified by God’s wrath. When the **melancholic** <term>complexion</term> <note>In Böhme’s time, "complexion" referred to the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile). When he does come, he comes either with harsh terror or as an angel—as friendly as a fawning little dog.

54. If he comes in the dark, and you are in a dark place, and he terrifies you, then do not move from his side; do not flee from him. He is not worthy of a human being giving way to him. Mock him in the darkness, saying:
> "Look, are you there? I thought you were an angel of light, yet you stand there lurking in the dark like a thief. There must be other places for you where there is more stench than here, since you only go about seeking the stench of sin."
Yet do not summon him to you, so that he is not given cause.

55. He does not easily terrify a defiant person who does not give way to him, especially one who is bold and mocks him. For he is proud and always wants to be master. If a person will not yield to him, he becomes annoyed and will not wait there.

56. But if he departs with a foul odor, then leave that place quickly, saying:
> "Fie! You stinking beadle-servant, how you smell of your lodging! It smells just like that in the **cloaca** <note>original: "Cloaca" - a sewer, latrine, or cesspool.</note>;"
He will not soon come to you again with terror.

58. In a moment of terror, do not look for many verses; he is too cunning for you, and he will tear the first and best one out of your heart so that you forget it or doubt it. Simply wrap your soul in this single one; it is strong enough to resist him. If you wrap your soul in it, you may well mock him; he cannot touch you and will not wait around for long. If you do not yield to him, he becomes a laughingstock before his other servants who attend to mankind, and also before the **Holy Angels**; he sees this above all things, even before you mock him.

59. Repeat the verse, take it into your heart, and draw a defiant courage against him; the Spirit that dwells within the verse will surely stand by you. Even if the soul trembles before him, stand in **wrath** <note>original: "Grimm." In Böhme’s work, "wrath" or "fierceness" can be a holy, protective fire used to repel the darkness of the devil.</note> against him as if you were risking your very life; nothing will happen to you. He is not allowed to use any power, nor does he have any; as long as a person lives in this time, he is not allowed to do anything to them. For **Christ** has opened the **Door of Grace**, which stands open to the poor sinner as long as he lives on earth; that same Door of Grace is open within the human soul.

60. **Christ** has shattered the firm castle (which was locked away in **God’s** wrath) within his own soul. Now all souls <term>interact</term> <note>original: "inqualiren." This is a specific term coined by Böhme, combining "inter," "quality," and "action." It describes how different forces or souls work within, influence, and flow through one another like the sap in a tree.</note> with one another; they all come from one, and together they are all but a single tree with many branches. His shattering of that lock has passed onto all souls, from him to **Adam** and to the very last human; the Door of Grace stands open to everyone. **God** has barred it to no one, except for the one who does not wish to enter. The sign of his entry into humanity is manifest to all souls; that will also be a testimony against the godless on the Day of Judgment: that they despised it.

# VIII. Treatise on Consolation

[...what] nature inflicts upon the poor soul, whether it be spiritual distress <term>Anfechtung: A central term in Böhme's theology, referring to a state of intense spiritual trial, doubt, or the feeling of being under God's wrath. Romans 8:26.

> This is my dear son, whom I had lost; he has come back; he was dead and has become alive.
How He ordered a feast to be prepared and rejoiced over his son who had been wicked; just as Christ further teaches that there is joy in the kingdom of heaven before the angels of God over one sinner who [repents]...

### VIII. Treatise of Consolation

81. Even if the soul does not attain this in this world, she shall receive it after this time, in the laying aside of this earthly tent <note>A biblical metaphor for the physical body and mortal life.</note>. However, it hides itself; for where He is most present, there He does not wish to reveal it; and if it should appear as though He does not want to be found, let no soul be terrified by this.

83. He hides it so that the soul shall knock and seek; for Christ says: "Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." <note>original: "Matth. 7, 7." Referencing Matthew 7:7.</note> My Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him for it. <note>original: "Luc. 11, 13." Referencing Luke 11:13.</note>

84. Let God’s promise be more certain to you; and even if your heart should say a loud "No," do not be terrified. For faith is not when someone receives joy in the fleshly heart or in the outer complexion <term>Complexion: In the medical and philosophical language of the 1600s, this refers to the four temperaments (choleric, melancholic, etc.) which Böhme believed governed the physical and emotional self.</term>, or when the mind becomes cheerful in the spirit so that heart and kidneys tremble with joy; this is not yet faith itself. These are merely the "love-rays" of the Holy Spirit—a divine glimpse that is inconsistent. For God does not dwell in the external heart or the complexion, but in Himself, in the other Center <note>Böhme envisions the human being as having multiple "centers" or levels of reality; the "outer" is the physical world, while the "inner" or "other" center is the eternal, spiritual realm.</note>, in the jewel of the noble image of the likeness of God; this is hidden from the external world.

85. True faith is when the soul-spirit, with its will and desire, enters into and longs for that which it neither sees nor feels. Understand this: the soul does not see what she purely encounters during this time; yet she sends her subtle will-spirit (which originates <note>original: "urständet" — a term Böhme uses to describe the arising or grounding of a spiritual force.</note> from her fire-life) into it. In that same will-spirit, the pearl is received, so that the soul-fire always remains in the desire. ### Of the Four Complexions

...a spark of Divine Love; it is the drawing of the Father <note>A reference to John 6:44: "No one can come to me unless the Father... draws them."</note> in His love.

86. The soul must stand firm in its desire, even when outer reason—speaking from the dark complexion <term>Complexion: One of the four temperaments (melancholic, phlegmatic, choleric, sanguine). Böhme argues that a "melancholic" or "dark" temperament can trick the mind into feeling abandoned by God.</term>—shouts a loud "No," claiming God is not there; for if He were not, there would be no desire or will for Him at all. For where God is not present in the spirit of the will, that spirit is blind and dead to God; it does not desire God, but lives only in opinions and does not care to seek Him. In such a person, there is only a subtle cleverness <note>literally "science" or "knowledge"</note> above other animals, simply because the soul is of a higher rank.

87. Therefore, a sorrowful heart must by no means allow the complexion to form the image in the heart that God is not there or present, or that He does not want the soul. Otherwise, the soul "eats" from such an imagination and becomes sorrowful. It is a great sin for the mind <note>original: "Gemüthe," referring to the emotional and dispositional center of a person.</note> to push such a fantasy into the heart: for the soul (being a noble creature from God's own nature) is agonized by it; the fantasy ignites the soul-fire so that it burns in such painful torment.

88. Dear mind, do not think otherwise when the anxiety of the complexion (ignited by the stars <note>Böhme believed the "constellations" or "stars" influenced the physical and seasonal shifts in human moods.</note>) arises: remember that you are then standing in God's vineyard. You must work and not stand idle; you do God a great service by it. Your work is to overcome through **faith**; even if no comfort appears in your outer heart, let nothing lead you astray.

89. Faith is not when I see; rather, **faith** is when I trust the hidden Spirit and believe His word, so that I would sooner lose my life than disbelieve His promise. Such a person truly wrestles with God, like the ancient Jacob throughout the night, who saw and felt nothing, but trusted in the promised word. He overcomes God, as was said to Jacob: *You have wrestled with God and with men, and have prevailed.* <note>original: "Gen. 32, 28." Referencing Genesis 32:28.</note> If you ask, "Which word is it?" The answer is: *My Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.* <note>original: "Luc. 11, 13." Referencing Luke 11:13.</note>

### VIII. Treatise on Consolation

*Luke 11:13.* <note>Though cited as Luke, the text follows the wording of John 16.</note> This is what the mouth of Christ himself said: "When he comes, he will lead you into all truth: for he will take from what is mine and declare it to you." *John 16:13, 14.*

90. But so that you do not doubt, be certain of this: that the temptation and the terror come only from the **temperament** <term>Complexion: One of the four "humors" or physical dispositions (Melancholic, Phlegmatic, Choleric, Sanguine). Böhme believed a person's physical makeup deeply influenced their spiritual experience.</term>; thus I present an **example** to you (one that may happen to a fiery **temperament**, and even more so to a **melancholic** one). If you walk at night in a dark room, you are terrified and always think there is something in the dark that might scare you; what kind of fear is that? Is the flesh afraid? No, otherwise it would not go there at all; the poor soul, imprisoned in the flesh, is afraid in the darkness and is always worried that the devil might grab her. For she knows that he dwells in the darkness, and thus the fear is that he will reach for her. There it is easily seen that the fear comes from the **imagination** <term>Phantasie: The mind's ability to form internal images. Böhme warns that the soul "eats" these images, meaning it is shaped by what it visualizes.</term>. It is the same for the poor soul in a perpetual, dark **chamber of temperament**; she is so timid because she must dwell in the dark, and she is always afraid of the devil and God's wrath.

91. A soul in the **Melancholic** chamber should by no means **speculate** <term>Speculation: Deep, probing intellectual or mystical inquiry. Böhme cautions that for a depressed person, such deep thinking can turn into a dangerous obsession with one's own perceived damnation.</term> on God's wrath, nor should they like to be alone, but rather stay among people who are talking; in this way, the soul imprints the **imagination** of the conversation on itself and does not **speculate**; for no **speculation** is useful to her; if she cannot apply it to her salvation, then let her leave it be.

92. Such a person should also not read such writings in which a **particular election** <note>original: "sonderliche Wahl." This refers to the Calvinist doctrine of predestination, which taught that God chooses some for salvation and others for damnation. Böhme argues this doctrine causes unnecessary despair.</note> is taught: they all teach without understanding and do not explain it correctly, as the high tongue of the Holy Spirit understands and has set it down, and as has been sufficiently demonstrated in our other writings.

93. He should not make use of many different writings, but should simply stay with the Scripture, where he may find a constant comfort.

94. But if he is endowed by God with a deep mind, so that the soul does not stop searching, then let him place himself in

96. A melancholic mind should guard itself with great earnestness against drunkenness, so that the soul is not too heavily burdened with earthly power. For when the body is so loaded with drink, the earthly power of the drink completely occupies the **chamber of temperament** <term>Complexion: A person's physical and psychological makeup. Böhme envisions these as "chambers" or rooms in which the soul dwells.</term>; then the soul imagines <note>In Böhme's vocabulary, to "imagine" is not just to dream, but to "form into an image" or to focus the soul's desire upon something.</note> into it, eats of the earthly distress, ignites her fire with it, and enjoys a little something therein. Then repentance begins in the soul, and she feels as though she were cursed.

97. Thus **God’s** wrath sets itself against her, as if he would push her into the root, into the center, into the darkness. Then the soul is anxious and seeks out those good drinking-brothers again, so that she might once more have a fool's joy. From this come the drinking-brothers who tie one day to the next and plunge their souls into **God’s** wrath and disgrace; this I say truthfully, as I have recognized high in the **Center of Nature** <note>original: "Centro Naturæ"</note> and in the **Principle** <note>original: "Principio"</note> of life.

For the melancholic chamber is rough, resembling the wild earth, and—

is almost desolate; it has a very weak hold on the **wheel of nature** <term>Wheel of Nature: Böhme’s term for the perpetual motion of the life-forces and emotions within a person. When balanced, it brings life; when agitated, it creates inner turmoil.</term>. When it happens that the fire of wrath is moved too much, the wheel of nature runs with a great clatter; just as one sees that the body trembles.

99. Since the **chamber of temperament** <term>Complexion-Kammer: The internal space of a person's psychological makeup. Böhme views the four temperaments (melancholic, phlegmatic, etc.) as "rooms" where the soul resides.</term> is so desolate and without substance, the wheel cannot easily be stopped again, and the senses cannot be gathered; instead, everything goes into confusion, completely fiery and fierce. The devil also likes to cast his **imagination** <note>For Böhme, "imagination" is the soul's power to focus on and "in-form" itself with either divine or worldly images.</note> into this state, so that great evil often occurs. This wheel looks into the outer spirit; but the poor soul then also eats from this turmoil, and things go terribly. Yet one should condemn no soul during such a time: for the **sign of the cross** still stands within her with an open **door of grace**.

100. The Melancholic chamber should guard itself against **greed**, and indeed depart from it with all earnestness: for it is as harmful to her as anger. Greed is an earthly desire, the temperament is also earthly, and the true chamber is almost desolate: then the desire pulls the earthly essence into the desolate chamber and fills it with such **dark matter** <note>original: "Materia"</note>, wherein nothing but bitterness and **God's wrath**, along with falsehood and injustice, are contained—an evil essence according to the property of the earth. This makes the temperament, because it is already an earthly desire, completely earthly.

101. From this, the poor soul then eats with her imagination, and subsequently feels in her fire-burning **God's severe judgment**, for He is angered by falsehood and injustice, as much of such base matter is introduced through greed. When the poor soul finds herself thus in **God's wrath**, she begins to doubt and despair: for she sees nothing around her but pure evil, earthly, false, and unjust things, from which only **God's wrath** is ignited.

## On the Choleric Temperament.

104. The person who has their best treasure, the noble soul, in a **Choleric house** <term>Cholerischen Hause: The "house" or "chamber" of the Choleric temperament, associated with the element of Fire and the qualities of heat and dryness.</term>, should above all things practice **humility** <term>Demuth: Humility is seen by Böhme as the spiritual "water" that cools the "fire" of the soul.</term>, or else they stand in great danger; they may well pour water into the fire, so that their noble image is not ignited: for this house yields great pride, stubbornness, sudden anger, and becomes nearly exalted, feared, and elevated, but is not dearly loved: unless the water of God, namely noble humility, enters the fire; then it is worthy of love and gives the first light.

105. For this chamber has its own shine in the outer nature: it is usually not humble, unless it has **Jupiter** in its sign of life, or **Venus**; yet even then, under Venus, it has its devil, who plagues it day and night with **unchastity** <note>original: "Unkeuschheit"</note>.

106. And I say as a warning, that there is great danger in this temperament, much greater than in the Melancholic. For here the devil comes in the **guise of an angel of light** <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 11:14, warning that spiritual deception can appear beautiful or righteous.</note>, in a fiery radiance; he tickles the poor soul so that she makes use of the fire-shine and becomes magnanimous; everything is presented to her as easy, and she bites very easily into sin; swearing, cursing, and light talk, which run against God's name and desecrate the soul, are not rare in this chamber; the fire's **fierce essence** <term>grimmige Essenz: The harsh, raw power of the soul's "fire" before it has been softened by divine love.</term> holds the mind back, so that it enters into God's love and gentleness (especially into true abstinence and repentance) with great difficulty; it always prefers to stare in anger, so that one should only fear it. Therefore be warned: become humble, apply yourself to gentleness in words and deeds, so that the temperament may not so easily ignite the soul: for a humble heart loves God. You are nothing more to God because of your temperament: only see to it that you do not misuse it; let everything happen for God’s glory, then nothing will harm you; break its will.

115. A lonely, quiet life would be good for you, but you are too expansive and find much, and you also give it away for free, like the air. Look to what you let in and what you give out, so that it is not the discovery of the stars <note>meaning: astrological or worldly influence</note>, but born of God; otherwise you will be deceived and you will deceive others.

### On the Four Temperaments.

116. You have a perilous path to walk here through the Sea of Misery <note>original: "Jammer-Meer"; a frequent metaphor in Böhme’s work for the suffering and spiritual danger of earthly existence.</note> within this temperament; you will constantly be defiled by the vices of words and deeds.

117. Water has a bright shimmer within it and gives a reflection, yet it is a false mirror: thus the poor soul within this temperament has a nearly unjust mirror; for water takes everything into itself, whether it be evil or good, it holds it, and becomes darkened by it.

118. So it is with this temperament: it absorbs the poisonous rays of all the stars and presents them as a mirror to the poor, captive soul; the soul then bites at this <note>The soul is tempted by the astral images, much like a fish is tempted by bait.</note> and carries out in the body that which is only a magical mirror-image within the temperament.

119. O, what good, sweet words—like sweet water—are offered without cost, yet they are mixed with bitter gall from the stars. There is almost no deceit too great: lies are the cloak of hypocrisy; to show oneself with a mirrored shimmer where "good Christians" reside in Babel <note>Böhme uses "Babel" to describe the confusion and hypocrisy of institutionalized, worldly churches.</note> is considered, and wants to be counted as, divine service.

120. You do not realize that you are doing wrong; but if someone comes too close to you with even a small spark, it is immediately reflected in your mirror. You would be well-advised to recognize that you are an ever-sinful human being: you should enter into true repentance and ask GOD for the governance of His Holy Spirit, so that the evil impulses <term>Affecten: From the Latin 'affectus,' referring to the passions or emotional states driven by the physical and astral nature rather than the spirit.</term> of the stars may be broken and kept in check, lest the poor soul embrace such things and thus become a fool.

121. A sober life will also be healthy for you. Constant vigilance and prayer, and always remaining in the fear of God—this turns away all evil from the stars. For he who lives according to the stars lives just like the cattle: but when one impresses the fear of God into the heart, the soul becomes a master over the external life and forces it into obedience; but if this does not happen, the temperament becomes the soul's master and guide. G. G. <note>Johann Georg Gichtel (1638–1710), a prominent mystic who was instrumental in collecting and publishing Böhme’s manuscripts.</note>, which<-

This supplement is a key to all the noble writings of this author, Jakob Böhme, by means of which one will—through God's gift—very soon arrive at the spirit of the writer, and be able to unlock the reins <note>original: "Nieren" (kidneys). In early modern and biblical language, the kidneys or "reins" were considered the seat of one's deepest emotions and hidden intentions.</note> and the heart, so as to soon discover the truth that lies within the reins along with the secret wisdom (in the heart). See Psalm 51:8 and Job 38:36 in the Hebrew <note>The author refers to these verses because they highlight God's desire for "truth in the inward parts" and "wisdom in the heart." In the Hebrew Masoretic text, Job 38:36 uses terms often associated with internal organs to describe the seat of intuition.</note>. A wise builder will also see and examine how far he has come with the construction of the house in the spirit, and what might still be lacking therein. In these maxims, he finds the resources for it in abundance and the account perfectly settled. The foundation is JESUS Christ himself, with the essential being <term>Wesenheit: A central term in Böhme’s thought, referring to the "substantiality" or "holy corporeality" of spiritual realities.</term> of love, from which the element of the spirit leads itself upward according to its forms (by virtue of diligent awakening and "digging deeper" in prayers); and these are the graces of sanctification, until we come entirely into God, He in us, and we in Him. May God give grace!

# The Incarnation of Jesus Christ. Part II.

1. Love and gentleness are our sword; they are the fire of the second principle <term>The second principle: In Böhme's system, this is the world of Light and Divine Love, as opposed to the first principle (the dark "fire" of God's wrath) and the third principle (the visible world).</term>, to which the devil and the world are enemies. Love looks into God; anger looks into hell. chapter 7, section 10.

2. Such knowledge is given to no one without wrestling <note>original: "Ringen" – a reference to Jacob wrestling with the Angel, symbolizing the spiritual struggle for enlightenment.</note>; yet not all reach the goal, though many seek eagerly. ch. 7, sec. 11.

3. A very great earnestness is now present, such as has never occurred since the world began. ch. 7, sec. 14.

4. It is not enough to pray: "Lord, give me a strong faith!" Instead, you must enter into Christ's suffering and death, and be born anew out of his death. ch. 7, sec. 15.

5. Our true life, with which we are meant to see God, is like a smothered fire; in many it is also like a fire locked within a stone <note>Böhme often uses the "fire in the stone" metaphor to describe the hidden spark of the Divine trapped within the "hard" material nature of the fallen human heart.</note>. We must strike it out through an earnest turning toward God. ch. 8, sec. 1.

6. How often does outward reason strike down that noble image which grows out of the bath of thorns <note>original: "Dornen-Bade" – a reference to spiritual growth that occurs through suffering and tribulation.</note> and through affliction! How many a branch is torn from the Pearl-tree <term>Pearl-tree: A recurring image in Böhme’s work representing the growth of the soul’s divine nature and the "Pearl" of great price (the Christ-spirit within).</term> through doubt and unbelief, which leads man onto the false path! ch. 8, sec. 5.

7. We have the center of nature within us: if we make an angel of ourselves, then that is what we are; if we make a devil of ourselves, then we are that as well. Here, we are in the process of "making" within the creation; we stand in the field. God’s will in love stands in the center <note>original: "Centro" (Latin: Center).</note> of life toward us. ch. 9, sec. 2.

8. Desire, sense, and mind hold the center of the spirit, from which the strong will is born; in this stands the right, true likeness and the image of God with flesh and blood—yet it stands in hiddenness. ch. 10, sec. 2.

9. The will is the root of the image; a false will destroys the image. The Incarnation of Jesus Christ, Part III. ch. 4, sec. 6.

## Aurora <note>original: "Morgenröthe" – Böhme’s first and most famous work, also known as "The Day-Spring."</note>.

The head contains within itself the five senses, in which the stars and elements qualify <note>original: "qualificiren" – a Böhme-specific term meaning to interact, influence, or imbue with specific qualities or powers.</note>, and therein arises

the Sidereal <term>Sidereal: Relating to the stars or constellations. In Böhme’s cosmology, the "sidereal spirit" is the psychological and natural spirit of man that is influenced by the celestial bodies.</term> Star-spirit or Nature-spirit within humans
and animals: in these, evil and good well up, and just as
the heavens make the stars, so the head makes the body
moveable. Chapter 2, Section 30.

2. In whichever quality you awaken the spirit, according to that
same quality do the thoughts rise up and govern the
mind <term>Gemüthe: A central term in German mysticism referring to the seat of the soul's disposition, emotions, and will.</term>. If you awaken the spirit in fire, then there wells
up in you bitter and hard wrath: for as soon as the fire
is ignited, which happens in hardness and fierceness,
the bitter fierceness wells up in the flash. Chapter 10,
Section 41.

3. Our life is like a constant war with the devil:
if he strikes me, I must retreat; but the
Divine power helps me up, then he also receives his
blow, and often loses the battle. But when he
is overcome, the Gate of Heaven opens in my
spirit. Then the spirit sees the Divine and Heavenly
Being; not outside the body, but in the source-fountain <note>original: "Quell-Brunne" – Böhme's term for the dynamic, bubbling origins of divine forces within the soul.</note>
of the heart the flash rises into the sensibility
of the brain, wherein the spirit speculates. The Holy Spirit
does not allow itself to be grasped or held in sinful flesh,
but it rises like a flash; however, when the flash is caught
in the source-fountain of the heart, it rises through the seven
source-spirits <term>Seven source-spirits: The seven foundational qualities (such as sourness, bitterness, heat, etc.) that Böhme believes constitute both the nature of God and the human soul.</term> into the brain like a dawn <note>original: "Morgenröthe" – This is the German title of Böhme's first book, *Aurora*. It represents the first light of spiritual recognition.</note>, and
therein lies the knowledge. Within this, the spirit sees
into the depth of the Godhead. This same God is just as much
in His Trinity in the body of holy souls as He is in heaven.
From this I take my knowledge, and I wish to know nothing
else but this same God, and He also creates the
certainty of my spirit, so that I constantly believe and
trust in Him. Chapter 11, Sections 67-71.

4. In this time, Love stands hidden in the center of the wrath-
fire, and Lucifer with his angels lies imprisoned in the
outward wrath-fire, until the judgment of God:
there he shall receive the wrath-fire, separated from Love,
as an eternal bath. Chapter 16, Section 54.

5. No man should think that the devil will be able to tear the
works of light out of his heart, for he can
neither see nor grasp them: and though he [is] in

6. And even though the devil cannot take the light away from
me, he still often covers it for me with the fleshly
birth, so that the sidereal <term>sidereal: Relating to the stars. Böhme believed the "sidereal spirit" was the bridge between the physical body and the eternal soul, influenced by the constellations.</term> birth is anxious, as if it were
imprisoned: these are all his blows, by which the grain of mustard seed <note>A reference to the parable of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:31), symbolizing the small but potent beginning of the Kingdom of God within the soul.</note>
is covered, of which Paul says in 2 Corinthians 12, verse 7, that

7. Because one part of your sidereal birth stands in wrath, and
the flesh stands in death through wrath, the devil
stands before you in the part of wrath constantly, right into your heart;
and if you give him room, he tears that part
of the sidereal birth which stands in love out of the
Word. Then your heart is a dark valley: if you
do not soon work again toward the birth of light, he ignites
the wrath-fire within it: then your soul is spewed
out of the Word and <term>inqualiret: A term Böhme coined from the Latin 'in-qualificare,' meaning the way an external force or quality permeates and becomes active within a being's inner nature.</term> permeated with the wrath of God;
and thereafter you are a devil, and with your soul-
birth you cannot reach the gate of heaven. Chapter 21,
Sections 46–47.

8. He who has love in his heart, and leads a mer-
ciful and gentle life, and fights against
malice, and breaks through the wrath of God into the light,
he lives with God and is one spirit with God. For God
requires no other service than that His creature, who
is in His body, does not move away from Him but is holy,
just as He is. Chapter 22, Sections 60–61.

9. When you worship God in His heaven, you worship
Him in the heaven that is in you: and that same God
breaks through your heart with His light, and within it the Holy Spirit, and
births your soul into a new body of God,
which reigns with God in His heaven. Chapter 24, Section 66.

### Of the Three Principles.

10. The whole Divine Being stands in constant and eternal

birth, but unchangeable, like the human mind, since thoughts are always born from the mind, and from the thoughts the will and desire, and from the will and desire the work, which is made into a *substance* in the will. Chapter 9, Section 35.

11. The *center* of the mind is free, and gives birth to the will from hearing and beholding; from this arises *imagination* and pleasure. Chapter 11, Section 10.

12. Adam was an image and complete likeness of God: his mind was a threefold spirit in the three *principles* <note>Böhme’s "Three Principles" refer to the dark fire-world (God's wrath), the light-world (God's love), and the physical world (the out-birth of the first two).</note> in one being. Thus his spirit and the will within the spirit should also have stood open in one being, as in the *paradisiacal* <note>original: *Paradiesschen*</note> state; his mind and soul were to eat from the heart of God, and the body from the power of the heavenly *limbus* <term>limbus: In Böhme's thought, the 'heavenly limbus' is the spiritual matter or 'holy flesh' of the divine realm, which was the intended food for the pre-Fall Adam.</term>. Chapter 11, Section 11.

13. Adam had the *matrix* <term>matrix: Refers to the feminine, generative principle. Böhme taught that the original Adam was androgynous, containing both male and female principles before the division into two sexes.</term> and also the man within him, and was meant to give birth from himself—as from the *matrix*—to the Virgin full of discipline and chastity. Chapter 12, Section 10.

14. Christ’s temptation to make bread out of stones was nothing other than this: Christ was meant to despise the bread of heaven—which man receives through faith and strong confidence in God—and set his *imagination* <note>In Böhme's vocabulary, 'imagination' is not just fantasy, but a creative, formative power that 'images' or shapes reality into the spirit.</note> into the spirit of this world and live within it. Chapter 12, Section 12.

15. The Adamite man can nonetheless live in *paradise* according to the inner *element* which stands open in the mind; if he resists malice and yields himself entirely with his whole power into the heart of God, then the Virgin <note>Refers to the 'Sophia' or Divine Wisdom, the spiritual counterpart to the soul in Böhme's mystical tradition.</note> dwells with him in the inner *element* in *paradise*, and enlightens his mind so that he can tame the Adamite body. Chapter 15, Section 20.

16. The first will is pure, neither dark nor light; but desire draws the *essences* of the stars and *elements* into itself, or into the spirit. Thus the will is filled with Divine power and led into darkness, which happens in the heart. This dark, anxious will then conceives another will for itself, to escape the anxiety and give birth to the light: and this second will is the mind, from which the senses emerge so as not to remain in this anxiety. Chapter 15, Sections 42–43.

17. Within our earnest mind, through the Word and power of God in the Crusher of the Serpent <note>original: "Schlangen-Treter," a reference to Christ, who according to Genesis 3:15 would crush the head of the serpent/devil.</note>, we can trample the head and will of the devil. Thus, the mind itself exists in free will, and it hovers in the power of God under His promise within a free being. Chapter 15, Section 44.

18. The mind <note>original: "Gemüthe"; in Böhme's thought, this refers to the inner disposition or the root of thoughts and desires.</note> in itself is the desiring will; however, the three <term>principles</term> <note>The "Three Principles" are the dark world of fire/wrath, the light world of love, and the physical world we inhabit.</note> possess and govern it. Chapter 16, Section 4.

19. The mind is whole and exists within being; the senses, however, are changeable and do not exist within being. Chapter 16, Section 5.

20. The mind is also the indissoluble bond which God—through the <term>Fiat</term> <note>Latin: "Let it be"; the divine creative command.</note>—breathed into Adam from the eternal mind in the welling spirit. Our eternal essences are only a particular part or spark from the eternal mind, which contains within itself the <term>center</term> of dispersal. Chapter 16, Section 6.

21. Within the mind lies the image of the spirit of the souls; whatever the mind inclines and gives itself toward, therein its soul-spirit is shaped by the eternal <term>Fiat</term>. Chapter 16, Section 49.

22. In this life, because the soul is contained in the will of the mind, you can shatter the gates of the deep and penetrate through to God by means of a new birth. Chapter 16, Section 53.

23. Everything you allow into your mind—if your soul is not inclined toward God so that it looks to Him in faith and confidence—is sin for you, whatever you do. For you lead an earthly mind into the gates of the deep where the Spirit of God moves, and you defile the <term>element</term> <note>In Böhme’s view, the "holy element" is the pure, spiritual substance of the heavenly world.</note> which is before God. Chapter 47, Section 78.

24. The sword of the <term>Cherub</term> <note>The angelic guardian placed at the entrance of Eden after the Fall.</note> is the kingdom or the portal of fierceness in the wrath of God, through which man must penetrate through the fierce death, through the <term>center</term>, into the other <term>principle</term>—into the paradise of the holy <term>element</term> before God. There, fierce death cuts away the earthly body (consisting of the four <term>elements</term>) from the holy <term>element</term>. Chapter 20, Section 45.

25. The <term>Cherub</term> is the Spirit of the Greater World <note>original: "Spiritus majoris Mundi"; the macrocosmic spirit or the spirit of the entire universe.</note>, and the earthly flesh is the sultry Garden of Eden. Chapter 20, Section 46.

26. Love does not penetrate into the wrath; rather, love is born out of the wrath and is entirely free. Christ does not enter into wrath again. Chapter 20, Section 75.

27. Delight is not entirely the mind; however, they are sibl— <meta>catchword: sibl- [from "Geschwister," meaning siblings or related]</meta>

It highlights the role of Christ and the "new birth" in overcoming the devil and returning to a spiritual, paradisiacal state.</summary>

27. Brothers and sisters. For when desire impregnates the mind <note>original: "Gemüth"; Böhme uses this term to describe the inner seat of the soul's desires and thoughts.</note>, it is already half a substance, and a breaking must follow, or it becomes a whole substance and the essence of a thing. Chapter 20, Section 88.

28. Man possesses the paths between the original will and the newly resolved will toward the Kingdom of Heaven; and each scale-pan is a maker, which makes whatever it allows into the mind. For the mind is the center of the balance, and the senses are the pivot that moves from one scale-pan to the other: one scale is the realm of fierceness <note>original: "Grimmigkeit," referring to the harsh, judgmental aspect of God's nature in Böhme's cosmology.</note> and wrath; and the other is rebirth in the power of God into the heavens. Whatever you allow into your mind through the senses, that is what takes effect. Chapter 21, Sections 23–26.

29. As we align ourselves with Christ through our senses and mind, the Father draws our soul—which exists in Him—into the pure love of Christ. There, through Christ, the soul once again places its <term>imagination</term> <note>For Böhme, "imagination" is not just fantasy, but the creative power of the soul to "image" or form itself into a spiritual reality.</note> before itself within the Holy Trinity, and is fed again by the Word of the Lord <note>original: "Verbo Domini"</note>. Thus it becomes an angel once more, purely separated from the kingdom of the devil and this world through the death of Christ. Chapter 22, Section 49.

30. The mind, if it is faithful, takes hold of the Godhead. Do not value yourself so lightly; if you are born in God, you are greater than this world. Chapter 22, Section 58.

31. At Jacob’s Well, Christ said to his disciples: "I have food to eat that you know nothing about. My food is to do the will of my Father in heaven." If God's will is His food, why should it not also be ours, if we live in Him? Did not Christ's divinity put on the Kingdom of Heaven as a body? Is not the pure element His body, in which the Godhead dwells? Chapter 23, Section 7.

32. The soul, surrounded by God, eats of God, for it is a spirit. Chapter 23, Section 11.

33. You must not stray from this will until you obtain the jewel <note>original: "Kleinod"; a term frequently used to represent the "pearl of great price" or the ultimate prize of spiritual enlightenment.</note>, even if it should last from day until night, and for many days more. If your earnestness is great, then the jewel you obtain through <term>overcoming</term> <note>The process of the soul's victory over its own dark, selfish impulses.</note> shall also be great. Chapter 24, Section 35.

34. Love in the new body is the prison of wrath in the old body: for the torment of wrath <note>original: "Zorn-Quall"</note> cannot enter into the love—

Love blossoms in the center of the soul, and within it, the Holy Trinity appears. Chapter 25, Section 16.

35. Love is God’s heart, and Wrath is His eternal strength; Love is His light, and Wrath is the eternal darkness, which creates another Principle where the devils reside. Chapter 25, Section 47.

36. Wrath is a root of life, and if it is without light, it is not God, but hellish fire; however, if the light shines within it, it becomes Paradise and a kingdom of joy. Chapter 25, Section 78.

37. A soul here in our body on earth does not possess the body of Christ in a tangible essence, but in the Word of power, which encompasses all: body and power are indeed one in Christ; however, we must not understand this as a physical creature in this world. Chapter 25, Section 89.

38. The knowledge of the ancients <note>Likely referring to pre-Christian philosophers or earlier spiritual seekers.</note> does not come from the <term>Holy Ternary</term> <note>original: "Ternario Sancto"; in Böhme’s thought, this refers to the divine manifestation, the "heavenly corporeality," or the "body" of the Trinity.</note>, from the body of Jesus Christ, but from the high eternity that reigns over the thrones. Chapter 25, Section 110.

### Appendix on the Principles

39. Every fire must have something to consume; of which there are two fires: in Love and in Wrath, as well as two eternal lives. Sections 32, 33.

40. Life reborn in love and life in the original source of torment are set against one another; because the life in love is not hostile, it must allow itself to be stung by thorns and crushed, and the cross is laid upon it to bear, in the patience of gentleness. Section 37.

### On the Threefold Life

41. The soul must go out from its own source of life and draw its will from the life of God; this same drawn will is accepted by God, and God dwells in that same will. Thus the divine light-life enters the soul and it is God's child. The other grasped will is called <term>Tincture</term> <note>original: "Tinctur"; a term borrowed from alchemy, referring here to a spiritual essence or "shining" that transforms and colors the soul's reality.</note>, for it is a radiance in the darkness. Chapter 1, Section 15; Chapter 4, Section 18.

42. The Divine Nature, from which the Divine Fire of Life burns, is infused with the love of God, so that the Light of God created another <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principium"; Böhme uses this term to describe different planes of reality or existence.</note> within itself, wherein no nature is felt, for it is the end of nature. Chapter 1, Section 21.

43. From the anxious will, the mind is formed; and from the <term>Wheel of Essences</term> <note>original: "Rad der Essentien"; this refers to the dynamic, revolving source of life and being in Böhme’s cosmology.</note>, the thoughts are born. Chapter 2, Section 40.

44. We must place our imagination and earnest will in God; then God appears to us in that will and fills the mind, so that we then feel God and see Him with our own eyes. Chapter 2, Section 51.

45. All words and works that are born out of the Eternal remain in the essence of the figure: for they cannot remain forever in spirit and power because they originated in the outer <term>Principle</term> <note>Referring to the physical or external world.</note>. Chapter 5, Section 132.

46. In the will of <term>reason</term> <note>original: "Vernunft"; often used by Böhme to describe limited, worldly human intellect as opposed to divine wisdom.</note>, we are children of the stars and elements, and the spirit of the world rules over us; but where we go out from this world’s will, the Spirit of God rules in us and confirms us as His children. Chapter 6, Section 32.

47. Whoever sets their will away from themselves and upon Christ, and lets go of all the reason of this world—however much it may shine—that person is reborn in Christ: their soul receives again the eternal flesh in which God became man, an incomprehensible flesh of the eternal essence. Chapter 6, Section 96.

48. If your will, along with all your reason and senses, is placed in God, refusing to let go of Him even if body and soul should shatter, then you hold fast to God; you break through death, hell, and heaven, and enter into the temple of Jesus Christ against all the resistance of the devils. God’s wrath cannot hold you, no matter how great and mighty it may be within you. Chapter 7, Section 13.

49. There is no other will in God but to save what is lost; therefore, no person should despair. For if the spirit of the soul rises up rightly, it is stronger than God and overcomes God—for the <term>Wrath</term> is also God’s, and is God’s greatest power, which the soul overcomes. It is stronger than the abyss of hell; it can move mountains without a storm, only by its will; for through the will, God created heaven and earth; and such a

50. That you doubt God's grace, of this you also have great sin: He is always merciful, and there is no other will in Him than to be merciful; He can do nothing else, His arms are spread day and night toward the poor sinner. Chapter 9, Section 29.

51. The birth of life reaches only the <term>Tincture</term> <note>In Böhme's alchemy, the Tincture is the spiritual "dye" or essence that transforms and gives life to matter.</note>, from which life burns; for whatever God wishes to reach must pass through the fire. Chapter 9, Section 71.

52. God leads your will, which is surrendered to Him, into the <term>Virgin of His Wisdom</term> <note>Also known as "Sophia," she represents the mirror of God’s glory and the feminine aspect of Divine Wisdom.</note>, so that you may behold all wonders: but you should not <term>imagine</term> <note>original: "imaginiren"; Böhme uses this to describe the soul's power to focus its desire and shape its reality, which can lead to spiritual error if directed away from God.</note> yourself into the wonders; as soon as you do that, you depart from God's will and are caught in your own imagination. Chapter 10, Section 48.

53. The image of God in man is so powerful and strong that, when it throws itself entirely into God’s will, it tames nature, so that the <term>stars</term> <note>original: "Gestirn"; Böhme believed the celestial bodies influenced the physical and psychological makeup of man, but a godly soul could overcome this influence.</note> are obedient to it, and rejoice greatly in that image. Chapter 11, Section 49.

54. If you turn from <term>Wrath</term> <note>original: "Zorn"; the dark, fiery foundation of existence in Böhme’s system.</note> into <term>Majesty</term> <note>The light-world or the loving, revealed side of God.</note>, you will be received as the dearest angel who never committed any sin; no sin will be recognized in you, but only God’s wondrous deed, which had to be revealed in the Wrath. For Love could not accomplish this in the fire: it does not mingle with the fire, but flees from it. Chapter 11, Section 62.

55. The worst enemy is our mind and senses, wherein the devil has his <term>fortress of prey</term> <note>original: "Raubschloß"; a metaphor for a robber baron's castle where the devil holds the soul's faculties captive.</note>, and great effort is required to drive him out. Chapter 12, Section 41.

56. When we pray to God, God hears our soul within ourselves in the <term>Center</term> <note>original: "Centro"; the inner core of the soul where it connects to the divine source.</note>; that is, the soul, with its repentant will, presses out from the center of anxiety, from the abyss of the soul, and also from the spirit of this world, into the inner <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principium"; a specific plane of reality or spiritual state.</note> in God, which is also within the soul. Chapter 16, Section 10.

57. The Word which created our soul has become man; it contains the Holy Spirit and meets the calling mind and will, opening itself from within the soul. Now, when the devil wants to [attack] the soul from below in the first <term>Principle</term>, in the Center of the four first <term>forms</term> <note>original: "Gestalten"; referring to the initial "forms of nature" that Böhme describes as the foundation of all being.</note>

58. The <term>stars</term> <note>original: "Gestirne"; Böhme refers to the astrological and cosmic influences that govern the physical body and the "outer" mind.</note>, which must rest in the Spirit of Christ, also lust to possess such a heart and soul where God’s Spirit has resided, for all creatures long for the power of God. 59. When we pray, we eat with the soul of many heavenly fruits, which have all grown out of the soul’s body as if from a heavenly field, and from this the soul eats again in prayer, and it is her food at God’s table. Chapter 16, Section 28.

60. The soul is created in heaven, in the <term>Matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrix"; used here to mean the "womb" or the generative source of Divine Love.</note> of love. Chapter 16, Section 30.

61. The will is the soul’s bridal carriage, with which she enters into the <term>Holy Ternary</term> <note>original: "Ternarium Sanctum"; Böhme’s term for the manifestation of the Trinity within the created spiritual order.</note>, wherein the Holy Spirit sits with the radiance of the Deity. Chapter 16, Section 31.

62. The soul should rule in all mysteries, but not let the devil in; because she runs into the will of the devil and the flesh, we are so full of doubt. Chapter 16, Section 33.

63. The will should thus be constantly set in God, so that it may go through the fire unscathed, and also through the outward Principle, such as through this world; and yet it should not allow itself to be captured or to lust after anything. Chapter 16, Section 36.

64. The soul is free from nature and is a lord of nature: for she is one spirit with God, and yet grows out of nature. She appears in Majesty with her power and radiance above the Center of the Heart, and has her own Principle in Majesty. Chapter 16, Section 37.

65. The soul has two forms: One is <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "Natura"</note>, and the other is the Divine flower or growth out of nature, which is above nature, as can be seen in the relationship between fire, light or radiance, and air. Chapter 16, Section 38.

66. The soul does not wish to enter into the <term>Wrath</term> <note>original: "Zorn"; in Böhme’s thought, the "Wrath" is the first, dark, fiery principle of God’s nature, associated with the father and the potential for hell if not tempered by light.</note>, for she knows the high-flying devil: thus she also does not gladly work in the spirit of this world, for it also veils God’s light from her. Chapter 16, Section 40.

67. When we pray, the will enters into the Word, and draws that into its hungry, thirsty, and parched soul, out of which a body grows. Chapter 16, Section 46.

68. Through prayer, the will enters into God; there it is filled with God’s power, which it then brings to the soul. Chapter 16, Section 48.

69. Christ's body is the number in the <term>Holy Ternary</term> <note>original: "Ternario Sancto"; the manifested triune being of God as it takes form in the spiritual world.</note>; and within this, the <term>Tincture</term> <note>original: "Tinctur"; an alchemical term used by Böhme to describe the spiritual life-essence or "dye" that transforms and vitalizes matter.</note> is heavenly: the number holds the cross, into which no creature can go; only the soul’s will enters therein: it is as subtle as God’s Spirit, and God’s Spirit also travels in the soul’s will—it is His carriage, which He holds dear. Chapter 16, Section 49.

70. The pure Godhead is Spirit, and as subtle as a will; but it became Man, and the subtle Spirit of God dwells within humanity, so that our souls may likewise reach God. Chapter 16, Section 50.

71. The body is taken from the <term>Fire- and Water-Center</term> <note>The "Centers" refer to the fundamental alchemical principles of the soul's composition.</note>. Chapter 17, Section 3.

72. The soul does not dwell thus in the external; rather, she is imprisoned by the external: her will has entered into the external and been made pregnant, and thus she eats in the <term>Center of Nature</term> <note>original: "Centro Naturæ"; the core of natural, temporal existence</note> and the external spirit of the earth. Chapter 17, Section 4.

73. External life stands in three parts: one is the <term>Starry Governance</term> <note>original: "Sternen-Regiment"; the astrological influences of the cosmos.</note>; the second is the governance with four forms—with fire, air, water, and earth; the third is God’s governance, for the Spirit of God hovers upon the water, upon the <term>Capsule</term> <note>original: "Capsula"; likely referring to the protective "husk" or vessel of creation.</note>, upon the <term>Matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrix"; the divine womb or generative source.</note>. Now, whichever person trusts God, and does not place his heart entirely in his own reason, has the Spirit of God always as his Creator; he possesses the <term>Word of Command</term> <note>original: "Verbum Fiat"; Latin for "The Word: Let it be done," the creative power of God.</note>, and creates continually. Chapter 17, Section 56.

74. Life stands in three parts: 1) The Inner, which is God’s eternal hiddenness in the fire. 2) The Middle, which has stood from eternity in God’s wonders as a likeness without essence. 3) The spirit <term>of the greater world</term> <note>original: "majoris mundi"; the macrocosm.</note>, in which figure the image became captivated and took on the external image. Chapter 18, Section 4.

75. The external <term>principle</term> <note>original: "Principium"; Böhme describes three "principles" or realms of existence: the dark fire-world, the light-world of God, and the visible, physical world.</note> exists only in the <term>solar tincture</term> <note>original: "Sonnen-Tinctur"; in Böhme's alchemy, this is the life-giving, spiritual essence of the sun that animates the physical world.</note>. Chapter 18, Section 5.

76. Mankind should have remained in God’s will and drawn from no other: for whatever the eternal <term>essences</term> <note>original: "Essentien"; the spiritual substances or "being-ness" that make up the inner world.</note> worked and opened within the fragile [body], should have stood eternally. The soul works in the center of her own will, and the <term>astral spirit</term> <note>original: "Sternen-Geist"; the "spirit of the stars" which Böhme believed governed the physical body, senses, and worldly instincts.</note> works in the body, in flesh and blood; it clings to the soul so that she lusts after it, acting just as the astral spirit does. Chapter 18, Section 9.

77. The soul does not dwell in the external spirit: though the external spirit has indeed woven itself into the soul like a <note>original: "Schalk"; a rogue, knave, or deceiver.</note> rogue; yet it does not possess the inner principle where the soul dwells; it is merely her covering and hindrance. Chapter 18, Section 13.

78. It is necessary to wake up—not by much searching [outside], but by seeking within oneself. Chapter 18, Section 14.

79. Two <note>original: "Suchten"; literally "cravings," "obsessions," or "drives."</note> cravings exist within the soul: one is the greedy, fierce fire-craving, which always seeks the earthly essence; and one is of the spirit, which is born out of the fire—this is God’s craving, and it seeks the Kingdom of Heaven. Chapter 18, Section 19.

80. The life of eternity is nothing but love alone. Chapter 18, Section 21.

81. The Devil is God’s <term>Wrath</term> <note>original: "Grimm"; the fierce, dark, and consuming quality of the first principle when it is not tempered by the light of God's love.</note> in the inner center, which is also the outermost: his kingdom is the darkness in nature. Mankind should bear a fruit from the soul-spirit by the power of the Holy Spirit: not according to the dark form of his earthliness, but out of the power of the light. Chapter 18, Section 22.

### Questions about the Soul.

82. The darkness does not swallow the light; rather, they are within one another. Question 1, Section 7.

83. The light has power; the darkness has <term>harshness</term> <note>original: "herbe"; a technical term for Böhme representing the first quality of nature: contraction, coldness, and sharpness.</note>, hardness, and cold. The desire of the will creates essences and attraction: and the light is sharpened within the sharp movement of the essence. Question 1, Sections 8–9.

84. In the inner, harsh desire, there is a sharp burning: therefore, the eternal fire is dark on the outside, but inward, in the will of eternal <term>freedom</term> <note>original: "Freyheit"; Böhme uses this to describe the "Ungrund" or the nothingness/potentiality of God before manifestation.</note>, it is a light that shines in the still eternity. Question 1, Section 11.

85. That which dwells alone in itself is called a <term>Principle</term>, and

that, within which it dwells, is called Nature, and it has seven spirits and forms. Question 1, Section 30.

86. The <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principium"; Böhme uses this to describe a fundamental realm or state of being—specifically the dark fire-world, the light-world, or the physical world.</note> has only one Spirit and Will, and is the power born out of the Will of Eternity. Question 1, Sections 31, 32.

87. What is within itself is not recognizable by itself, but can be well felt according to the spirit. Question 1, Section 33.

88. Leave your deep rational-searching and go into God’s will, into God’s spirit; then your will is God’s will, and God’s spirit will seek you within yourself. And if He finds your will in Him, He reveals Himself in your will as His own property. Let no fear terrify you: there is nothing that can take [Him] away except your <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Imagination"; in Böhme’s thought, this is not just "fantasy" but the creative power of the mind to "form" its own reality and attach itself to worldly or spiritual things.</note>; do not leave that in the will, and so you will work God’s wonders in His spirit. Question 1, Sections 36, 37, 38.

89. Seek the first root of the soul in the fire-life, and the second in the light-life in the Majesty; thus you will find God’s image and likeness, in which the greatest mysteries of the Godhead lie. Question 1, Section 56.

90. The Single Spirit separates into two <term>principles</term> or two spirits, but not in a divided way, and yet fleeing from one another. Question 1, Section 65.

91. The eternal fire burns eternally; it is, however, a spirit and is not manifest in a <term>fierce</term> <note>original: "grimmige"; referring to "Grimmigkeit" or the wrathful, harsh quality of the dark fire-world.</note> way in the Kingdom of God. Question 1, Section 91.

92. The light also desires the <term>fire-source</term> <note>original: "Feuer-Quall"; a term Böhme coined to combine "source" (Quelle) and "torment" (Qual), describing the agonizing tension that generates life and light.</note>, namely for the gentleness and power within itself; the light is also a fire. The fire’s fierceness and the light’s radiance are two principles, two kinds of source-torment: each dwells within itself, and neither comprehends the other, even though one is the life and cause of the other. Question 1, Section 92.

93. In the fire there can be no true understanding, but rather in the desire of the light: therefore the fiery will must turn to God’s heart, as to the power of light and understanding. Question 1, Section 123.

94. The noble image greens <note>The author uses the metaphor of a plant growing or "greening" (grünet) to describe spiritual growth.</note> out from the soul-fire, like a flower from the earth, and has no feeling of the fiery quality; for the fire stands within it as if swallowed up, and though it is indeed there, it is in another quality—as the desire of love, a light-flaming fire in the Divine quality. Question 1, Section 126.

95. The <term>Image</term> <note>original: "Bildniß"; in Böhme's thought, this is the eternal, spiritual archetype of man created in God's likeness.</note> stands outside of all <term>torment</term> <note>original: "Quall"; Böhme often uses this word to describe the "agony" or "tension" inherent in the birth of nature.</note>, and dwells only within itself, and God through it, like the apple on the tree, to which the sun gives strength. Question 1, Section 127.

96. If the spirit of the will turns itself into the death of Christ, and yet is also violently bound to the <term>wrath</term> <note>original: "Grimm"; the fierce, dark quality of God's fire-nature.</note>, it hangs like a thread upon the death of Christ. This soul must indeed burn for a while in this way, until the spirit of the will can enter into the death of Christ, until its <term>siderial wood</term> <note>original: "siderisch Holz"; the "astral" or planetary influences that make up the temporary, earthly personality.</note> is burned away: for it has lost body and essence, and stands purely in God’s mercy in the Divine <term>Tincture</term> <note>original: "Tinctur"; an alchemical term used by Böhme to describe the spiritual life-blood or essence that transforms and heals.</note>, as in the Number 9. Question 1, Section 140.

97. The new man, born in God, will possess the Eternal, for he has gone out from the fragile and has put on God in Christ; he possesses God’s body within the Old. Question 1, Section 247.

98. God’s will is only love: but the <term>Turba</term> <note>original: "Turba"; a technical term in Böhme’s writing meaning the "disturber" or the awakening of God's wrath that destroys any form that has turned away from the light.</note> is His wrath-will, which with its fierce hunger has brought a great kingdom of its revelation into its wonders, such as the devils and godless souls. Question 1, Section 252.

99. The true <term>fire-smith</term> <note>original: "Feuer-Schmid"; the soul acting as the creative, forging power within the human being.</note> (the soul) sits in the heart and conducts his rule with the spirit in the head; there he has his council house, as the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "Gemüth"; the deep disposition or inner seat of the soul's desires.</note>, and the five princely councilors, as the five senses, which arise from the five spirits of the understanding. Treatise 11, Section 5.

100. God’s light does not go backward, but forward into eternity. Treatise 12, Section 7.

101. The Image of God is magical and as subtle as a spirit, and yet much subtler, yes, much subtler and thinner than the soul itself: it is like God, who dwells in the eternal freedom, for He is thinner than "Something." So too is your noble Image, which nevertheless stands in heavenly flesh and blood, and is essence out of God’s body: it is Christ’s flesh and blood, and your soul dwells within it. Within it, she is the fire of Majesty, and the Holy Spirit sits in the heart of the Image, and goes out from the Image with voices, languages, etc. Treatise 12, Sections 23, 24.

102. The will makes the sin; it comes from the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Imagination"; here meaning the power of the mind to "form" or "image" itself into a thing.</note> in the spirit; the spirit enters into a thing and becomes infected. Treatise 15, Section 4.

103. Everything is sin that desires to lead the external into the internal (within the will). The will should be directed purely toward love and gentleness, as if it were nothing or dead; it should desire only God’s life, so that God may work within it. In everything else it does, its will should be so directed that it does it for God; for if it places its will into <term>essence</term> <note>original: "Wesen"; here meaning the material or self-centered substance of the world</note>, it leads that essence into the spirit, which then takes possession of its heart: thus the <term>Turba</term> <note>original: "Turba"; a Latin term Böhme uses for the "disturber" or the power of wrath and confusion that destroys harmony.</note> is born. Fr. 15. §. 5.

104. In the spirit, born out of the soul, dwells the <term>Image of God</term> <note>the spiritual archetype of humanity</note> with the Divine Virgin of the Wisdom of God <note>Sophia, the mirror of God's glory</note>. For in the spirit lies all understanding and intellect: it possesses the senses and the noble life that unites itself with God, and it is so subtle that this spirit can and may enter into God. If this spirit gives itself over to God, and casts away its soul’s fire-glory and cleverness, it attains God’s Image and God’s body; for it enters into God with the will, and dwells with power in God; thus it takes God’s <term>essence</term> upon itself, and is outside of this world in the life of God. F. 37. §. 9.

### The Converted Eye.

105. The soul is an entire likeness and image of the Holy Trinity, if one understands the soul as the <term>Center of Nature</term> <note>original: "Centrum Naturæ"</note> and its fire-life as the <term>First Principle</term> <note>original: "1. Prinipium"; the foundational source of energy or "fire" in Böhme's cosmology.</note>. But the soul’s outgrowth or Image, which is a likeness of God, grows out of the soul like a flower out of the earth, and is seized by the Holy Spirit, for it is His dwelling-house. When the soul sets its <term>imagination</term> <note>the power to form or "image" oneself</note> out of the <term>fire-torment</term> <note>original: "Feuer-Qual"; the state of agitation or longing in the soul</note> and into the light of God, it receives the light, just as the moon receives its shine from the sun. Thus its Image stands in the majesty of God, and the soul in the light of God, and its fire-torment is transformed into a gentleness and a desiring love, where it is then recognized as God's will. §. 6.

### The Incarnation of Jesus Christ, Part 1.

106. Whoever desires to enter into God’s love enters with his will-spirit into Paradise: there, Paradise greens again in his will-spirit, and [he] receives...

107. Adam and Eve went out of heaven into this evil, corrupted world, into the house of sin; there, immediately in their mind at the *Center of Nature* <note>original: "Centro Naturæ"; the foundational, restless source of existence in Böhme’s cosmology</note>, the wheel of the senses began to *operate* <note>original: "qualificiren"; to interact or take on specific qualities/powers</note> in earthly torment, where each sense was opposed to the other. ch. 7, §. 4.

108. Just as the air and the water fill this world, and we all enjoy them; so in secret is the Divine Essence, which we enjoy if we earnestly *imagine* <note>original: "imaginiren"; in Böhme’s sense, this is a deep, creative spiritual focusing or "inward molding" of the soul</note>, and surrender ourselves into it with the will. ch. 8, §. 10.

109. The devil also sets his *imagination* with his false *tincture* <note>original: "Tinctur"; a spiritual life-force or transformative essence</note> into love, and poisons the soul's best jewel, just as he then infected Adam’s soul with his *imagination*. ch. 11, §. 4.

110. Out of **God’s** wrath-fire, the new man must sprout forth. ch. 12, §. 22.

## The Incarnation of **JESUS Christ**, Part 2.

111. It costs much to wrestle with **God’s** wrath and triumph over the devil: if we did not have Christ with us there, we would lose the battle. ch. 5, §. 16.

112. We must do good for evil and love one another, as Christ did for us and gave His life for us in death. If we do this, we also extinguish **God’s** wrath in our neighbor. ch. 5, §. 17. 18.

113. While the earthly man lives, the soul is always in danger: for the devil is at enmity with it, always shooting his rays with false *imagination* into the spirit of the stars and elements, thereby grasping at the soul-fire, constantly wanting to infect it with earthly, devilish addiction; there the noble image must defend itself against the soul-fire: there it costs a struggle for the angel's little crown. ch. 6, §. 11.

103. Everything is sin that desires to bring the external into the internal (into the will). The will should be directed solely toward love and gentleness, as if it were nothing or dead; it should only desire **God’s** life, so that **God** may work within it. In everything else it does, the will should be so directed that it does it for **God**; for if the person places their will into the <term>essential being</term> <note>original: "Wesen"; the substance or material manifestation</note>, they lead that being into the spirit, which then takes possession of the heart: thus is the <term>Turba</term> <note>original: "Turba"; in Böhme’s thought, this refers to a state of spiritual disturbance, turmoil, or the "awakener" of God's wrath within the soul</note> born. Forty Questions 15. §. 5.

104. In the spirit, born out of the soul, dwells the image of **God** with the Divine **Virgin of Wisdom** <note>original: "Göttlichen Jungfrauen der Weisheit"; often referred to as Sophia, representing the mirror of God’s glory and the feminine principle of divine wisdom</note>. For in the spirit lies all understanding and <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: "Witz"; in this historical context, it refers to intellectual capacity or ingenuity rather than humor</note>: it possesses the senses and the noble life that unites with **God**, and is so subtle that this spirit can and may enter into **God**. When this spirit surrenders itself to **God**, and casts away the soul’s fire-pomp and cleverness, it attains **God’s** image and **God’s** body; for it enters into **God** with the will, and dwells with power in **God**; thus it takes on **God’s** essence and is outside of this world in the life of **God**. F. 37. §. 9.

### ->The Turned Eye.<-

105. The soul is a complete likeness and image of the Holy Trinity, if one understands the soul as the *Center of Nature* <note>original: "Centrum Naturæ"</note>, and its fire-life as the First Principle. But the soul's outgrowth or image, which is a likeness of **God**, grows out of the soul like a flower from the earth, and is seized by the Holy Spirit, for it is His dwelling house. When the soul sets its <term>imagination</term> <note>deep spiritual molding or inward focusing</note> out of the fire-torment into **God’s** light, it receives the light, just as the moon receives the sun's brilliance. Thus its image stands in the majesty of **God**, and the soul in **God’s** light, and its fire-torment is transformed into a gentleness and a desiring love, where it is then recognized as **God’s** will. §. 6.

Chapter 10, §. 8.
